episodes.logline: Her coins call her Sultan, and for four fierce years Razia governs in her own name while nobles fear the woman they cannot control.
episodes.moral: A rightful voice may sound revolutionary in an unjust room.

sources.citation: Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, account of Razia's reign
sources.note: Principal near-contemporary narrative, shaped by elite court assumptions.

sources.citation: Coins of Razia with Arabic and Nagari legends, Indian Museum and American Numismatic Society examples
sources.note: Primary evidence that she used the sovereign title Sultan.

sources.citation: K.A. Nizami, 'Razia Sultana', Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd edition; Peter Jackson (2003)
sources.note: Modern correction of the title and critical reading of the succession story.

episodes.notes: After Iltutmish's death, Razia displaced Ruknuddin Firuz in November 1236, ruled directly, appointed Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut as Master of Horses, fought rebel governors, was overthrown after Malik Altuniya's revolt, and died in October 1240 while trying to regain Delhi. Her coins are the strongest evidence for her authority and for using Sultan rather than Sultana. Recent numismatic and gender-history work emphasizes sovereign titulature over romance. Do NOT claim a love affair with Yaqut, do NOT present unveiling stories as certain, and do NOT call her merely queen-consort.

episodes.title: Balban Builds the Shadow of God
episodes.region: Delhi, Multan and the Mongol frontier
episodes.logline: A former slave turns kingship into ceremony, spies on governors, breaks the Forty, and loses his heir defending Delhi from the Mongol storm.
episodes.moral: Fear may guard a throne, but it cannot soften grief.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, 14th century
sources.note: Main source for Balban's court ritual, spies and noble politics.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Qiran-us-Sadain, 1289, and elegies for Prince Muhammad
sources.note: Courtly evidence from a poet close to Balban's family.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (2003), chapter on Balban
sources.note: Critical reassessment of absolutism and frontier defense.

episodes.notes: Balban rose from enslaved Ilbari Turk to regent and then sultan, ruling from 1266 to 1287. Barani credits him with crushing the old corps of Forty, enforcing sijda and paibos, using barids as intelligence officers, and guarding the northwest; his son Prince Muhammad was killed fighting Mongols in 1285. Jackson cautions that Balban's absolutism was real but not absolute, since noble cooperation still mattered. Do NOT turn Barani's claim that Balban never laughed into literal biography, and do NOT imply his reforms permanently ended factional politics.

episodes.title: Malik Kafur Marches Beyond the Vindhyas
episodes.region: Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai and Delhi
episodes.logline: Bought for a thousand dinars, Malik Kafur leads Alauddin's armies across the Deccan and returns with tribute that changes Delhi's imagination of India.
episodes.moral: A meteoric rise can dazzle and destroy.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, 1311
sources.note: Contemporary panegyric account of Alauddin Khalji's campaigns.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
sources.note: Later Persian chronicle, useful but less detailed on the Deccan raids.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan 1300-1761 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
sources.note: Modern context for Deccan politics and Sultanate pressure.

episodes.notes: Malik Kafur, captured in Gujarat in 1299 and later Alauddin Khalji's trusted commander, led tribute-seeking campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal, the Hoysalas and the Pandyas between 1307 and 1311. These raids extracted wealth and submission but did not annex the south permanently, and Kafur was killed soon after briefly dominating politics after Alauddin's death in 1316. Recent Deccan scholarship stresses local agency and long-term political consequences. Do NOT claim he conquered south India, and do NOT state that the Koh-i-Noor was certainly taken at Warangal; that is later tradition, not contemporary evidence.

episodes.title: Alauddin Holds Siri Against the Mongols
episodes.era: Khalji wars with the Mongols, 1297-1306 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Siri, Kili, Amroha and the Ravi frontier
episodes.logline: Five times the Mongols press toward Delhi, and Alauddin answers with forts, armies, hard discipline, and the city of Siri.
episodes.moral: A city survives when preparation outlasts panic.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi
sources.note: Main narrative source for the Mongol invasions and Kili.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Nuh Sipihr, 1318
sources.note: Courtly celebration of Alauddin's victories and Delhi's world.

sources.citation: Banarsi Prasad Saksena, 'Alauddin Khalji', in A Comprehensive History of India, Vol. 5 (1970); Jackson (2003)
sources.note: Detailed modern analysis of chronology and exaggerated army figures.

episodes.notes: Between 1297 and 1306, Alauddin's forces faced repeated Chagatai Mongol attacks, including Kili in 1299, the siege of Siri in 1303, Amroha in 1305 and fighting near the Ravi in 1306. Zafar Khan's death at Kili became heroic memory, while the 1303 siege exposed Delhi's food vulnerability and helped drive later market controls. Recent historians treat Barani's huge numbers as symbolic or inflated and emphasize fortification, logistics and Chagatai politics. Do NOT claim Alauddin personally charged into battle or that he ended all Mongol danger forever.

episodes.title: Muhammad bin Tughlaq Tests the Impossible
episodes.region: Delhi, Daulatabad, the Deccan, Sindh and Himalayan frontiers
episodes.logline: A brilliant sultan moves a capital, issues token coins, dreams across mountains, and leaves Ibn Battuta amazed by genius and terror in the same court.
episodes.moral: Vision without workable trust can ruin what it hopes to save.

sources.citation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, India sections dictated c. 1355
sources.note: Eyewitness account from a qadi at Muhammad bin Tughlaq's court.

sources.citation: Billon and base-metal token coins of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in museum collections
sources.note: Physical evidence for the failed fiduciary currency experiment.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (2003), chapter on Muhammad bin Tughlaq
sources.note: Modern critique of the old 'mad sultan' caricature.

episodes.notes: Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled from 1325 to 1351 and attempted a capital transfer to Daulatabad around 1327, a token currency around 1329-1332, and ambitious frontier campaigns. Ibn Battuta portrays a ruler of learning, generosity and cruelty; coins prove the currency experiment, and Deccan history shows the capital move helped seed durable Muslim communities even as it caused suffering. Recent scholarship rejects mental-illness caricatures and sees failed implementation of strategic ideas. Do NOT claim he killed his father as fact, that he reached China, or that he was simply insane.

episodes.title: Timur Leaves Delhi Empty
episodes.era: Timurid invasion of north India, 1398-1399 CE
episodes.region: Delhi, Punjab, Gujarat and Samarkand
episodes.logline: Timur storms into a weakened Sultanate, sacks Delhi in December 1398, and marches away with treasure, captives and artisans for Samarkand.
episodes.moral: A city divided within is most vulnerable to the storm outside.

sources.citation: Yazdi, Zafar Nama, 1424-1425, translated in Elliot and Dowson, History of India, Vol. III
sources.note: Official Timurid account of the Indian campaign.

sources.citation: Tuzuk-i-Timuri / Malfuzat-i-Timuri traditions
sources.note: Timurid court memory of the campaign, including the prisoner massacre, with authenticity caveats.

sources.citation: Beatrice Forbes Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (Cambridge University Press, 1989/1999)
sources.note: Standard modern biography for Timur's aims and methods.

episodes.notes: In 1398, after years of Tughlaq decline, Timur entered India, ordered a mass killing of prisoners before the battle, took Delhi in December, looted for days, enslaved artisans, and left rather than ruling. Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Tughlaq fled, and Delhi's political center never regained the reach it had under earlier sultans. Modern scholarship accepts the catastrophe while warning that exact death totals come from rhetorical chronicles. Do NOT claim precise casualty figures as census data, and do NOT attach the Koh-i-Noor legend to Timur's Delhi sack as fact.

episodes.title: Stone Speaks at the Qutb Complex
episodes.era: Qutb Complex building phases, c. 1193-1368 CE
episodes.region: Mehrauli, Delhi
episodes.logline: Across 170 years, masons, calligraphers and sultans turn reused columns, true arches, domes and repairs into the first great archive of Sultanate stone.
episodes.moral: Monuments remember collaboration as well as conquest.

sources.citation: Qutb Complex inscriptions of Aibak, Iltutmish, Alauddin Khalji and Firuz Shah Tughlaq
sources.note: Primary site evidence for building phases and repairs.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi, List No. 233
sources.note: Authoritative conservation and monument description.

sources.citation: Finbarr Barry Flood, Objects of Translation (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Recent study of material reuse and Indo-Islamic craft translation.

episodes.notes: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque reused material from multiple Hindu and Jain temples; Aibak began the minar, Iltutmish completed the core tower and tomb, Alauddin added the Alai Darwaza in 1311 and began the unfinished Alai Minar, and Firuz Shah repaired the damaged top in 1368. The Alai Darwaza is central to the story of true arch and dome technology in India, though earlier corbelled forms complicate easy firsts. Recent Flood scholarship asks writers to avoid one-note vandalism or one-note harmony. Do NOT say Aibak completed the tower, or that the mosque came from a single temple.

episodes.title: Alauddin Fixes the Price of Wheat
episodes.region: Delhi, Siri and the grain routes of the Doab
episodes.logline: After siege hunger frightens Delhi, Alauddin fixes prices, licenses traders, fills granaries and posts spies so an enormous army can eat cheaply.
episodes.moral: Order can feed a city, but coercion has a cost.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, account of Alauddin's market regulations
sources.note: Most detailed source for fixed prices, spies, granaries and punishments.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, 1311
sources.note: Contemporary court account giving a more benevolent explanation.

sources.citation: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part I (2007)
sources.note: Modern university-level synthesis of the reforms and their purposes.

episodes.notes: Alauddin's system regulated grain, cloth, animals, slaves and general commodities through mandis, Sera-i-Adl, state transporters, granaries, market officers and barid spies. Barani links low prices to cheap army maintenance after Mongol pressure; Khusrau frames it as welfare, and modern historians often see both motives. The system lasted roughly until Alauddin's death in 1316 and was quickly dismantled, implying strong merchant resentment. Do NOT call it the world's first price control; say it was among the most systematic state market interventions in recorded medieval India, and do NOT present it as purely benevolent.

episodes.title: Firuz Shah Turns Water into Villages
episodes.region: Delhi, Hauz Khas, Feroz Shah Kotla, Punjab and Haryana canal zones
episodes.logline: Firuz Shah digs canals, restores tanks, founds villages, moves Ashokan pillars, and writes a memoir that lists both welfare works and hard-edged intolerance.
episodes.moral: Public works shine brightest when remembered with honesty.

sources.citation: Firuz Shah Tughlaq, Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi, translated in Elliot and Dowson, Vol. III
sources.note: Rare first-person royal account of canals, hospitals, villages and punishments.

sources.citation: Shams-i-Siraj Afif, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, c. 1398
sources.note: Main narrative source for Firuz Shah's reign.

sources.citation: ASI documentation of Hauz Khas, Feroz Shah Kotla and the Ashokan pillars in Delhi
sources.note: Material evidence for his building and monument-moving projects.

episodes.notes: Firuz Shah ruled from 1351 to 1388 and emphasized restoration after Muhammad bin Tughlaq's turbulence: canals, more than 300 villages in his own claims, sarais, hospitals, madrasas, Hauz Khas works, and the transport of Ashokan pillars to Delhi. His Futuhat is invaluable because a sultan speaks in first person, but it also records religiously harsh policies, executions and a large slave establishment. Recent environmental and heritage work has renewed attention to medieval hydraulics. Do NOT portray him as purely benevolent, and do NOT claim his anti-torture statements erased all brutality.

episodes.title: Amir Khusrau Sings Hind and Iran
episodes.region: Patiyali, Delhi, Multan, Bengal and Nizamuddin
episodes.logline: Serving eight sultans and loving one saint, Amir Khusrau writes Persian for courts, Hindavi for the street, and songs that still echo at Nizamuddin.
episodes.moral: A bridge of words can outlive empires.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, Qiran-us-Sadain, Nuh Sipihr and Tughlaq Nama
sources.note: Surviving works that make Khusrau both poet and historical witness.

sources.citation: Amir Hasan Sijzi, Fawaid-ul-Fuad, compiled 1309-1322
sources.note: Conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya with references to the Chishti circle.

sources.citation: Sunil Sharma, Amir Khusraw: The Poet of Sultans and Sufis (Oneworld, 2005)
sources.note: Key modern English biography and literary guide.

episodes.notes: Khusrau, born in 1253 to a Turkic father and Indian mother, served courts from Balban's circle to the Tughlaqs, wrote major Persian masnavis and histories, celebrated India in Nuh Sipihr, and became inseparable from Nizamuddin Auliya's Chishti world. His Hindavi verses, riddles and musical memory helped shape later north Indian culture, while qawwali tradition keeps him alive at the dargah. Recent musicology warns that sitar and tabla invention stories are late. Do NOT claim he invented the sitar or tabla, and do NOT state Khaliq Bari is certainly his without caveat.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Words, Song and the Open Door

episodes.title: Nizamuddin Opens the Khanqah Door
episodes.region: Badaun, Ghiyaspur, Delhi and the Nizamuddin Dargah
episodes.logline: While sultans summon and threaten, Nizamuddin Auliya keeps his khanqah open to the poor, the stranger and the singer at the edge of Delhi.
episodes.moral: Service can become a kingdom without a throne.

sources.citation: Amir Hasan Sijzi, Fawaid-ul-Fuad, translated as Morals for the Heart by Bruce B. Lawrence (1992)
sources.note: Primary record of Nizamuddin's conversations, ethics and social world.

sources.citation: Simon Digby, 'The Sufi Shaykh and the Sultan', Iran 28 (1990)
sources.note: Modern study of competing saintly and royal authority.

sources.citation: Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, Sufi Martyrs of Love (Palgrave Macmillan, 2002)
sources.note: Context for the Chishti order in South Asia.

episodes.notes: Nizamuddin Auliya, born in Badaun in 1238 and dead in Delhi on April 3, 1325, made Ghiyaspur a Chishti center where food, counsel and song crossed lines of status and community. Fawaid-ul-Fuad records teachings on poverty, love, music and distance from rulers; later tradition dramatized his conflict with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq through the phrase 'Delhi is still far away.' Recent scholarship treats the khanqah as both spiritual refuge and social institution, not an apolitical fantasy. Do NOT present the curse story as established fact, and do NOT claim the Chishtis had no links at all to Sultanate political economy.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Words, Song and the Open Door

episodes.title: The Yuezhi Cross a Thousand Mountains
episodes.era: Yuezhi migration and settlement in Bactria, c. 176-30 BCE
episodes.region: Gansu, the Ili Valley, Sogdia and Bactria
episodes.logline: Driven from the grasslands by Xiongnu power, the Greater Yuezhi cross Central Asia and settle in Bactria, where one clan will become the Kushans.
episodes.moral: A people in exile can carry the seeds of a new world.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji, chapter 123, Zhang Qian's mission
sources.note: Earliest outside account of the Yuezhi in Bactria and their five-part political structure.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu, chapter 88, trans. John Hill, Through the Jade Gate to Rome (2009)
sources.note: Chinese account of the Yuezhi defeat, migration and later Kushan rise.

sources.citation: Craig Benjamin, The Yuezhi: Origin, Migration and Conquest of Northern Bactria (2007)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the migration and Bactrian settlement, with caution on ethnicity.

episodes.notes: The Greater Yuezhi were forced west after Xiongnu attacks around 176-174 BCE, moved through the Ili region, displaced Sakas, and entered Bactria around the mid-2nd century BCE. Zhang Qian found them settled and prosperous about 128 BCE, divided among five yabghu groups, one of which was Guishuang, the later Kushan clan. RECENT FINDINGS: modern Central Asian archaeology and ancient-DNA work have made older simple identifications with Tocharians insecure. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the Yuezhi were definitely Tocharian; do NOT confuse them with later Mongol movements; the skull-cup story is in Chinese sources but cannot be archaeologically verified.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Kujula Kadphises Forges the Kushan Crown
episodes.era: Founding of the Kushan dynasty, c. 30-80 CE
episodes.region: Bactria, Kabul, Gandhara and Taxila
episodes.logline: Kujula Kadphises unites the five Yuezhi chiefs, borrows the coin language of Greeks and Indians, and turns a migrant clan into a kingdom.
episodes.moral: A founder succeeds by joining old loyalties to new ambition.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu, chapter 88, trans. John Hill (2009)
sources.note: Primary Chinese narrative of Kujula attacking the other yabghu and founding Guishuang rule.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, published by Joe Cribb and Nicholas Sims-Williams, JONS 160 (1995/96)
sources.note: Names Kujula as the great-grandfather of Kanishka and anchors the dynasty.

sources.citation: Osmund Bopearachchi, Monnaies greco-bactriennes et indo-grecques (1991); Joe Cribb and David Jongeward coin studies
sources.note: Key numismatic work on Indo-Greek, Indo-Parthian and early Kushan transitions.

episodes.notes: Kujula Kadphises, the Guishuang yabghu, probably united the Yuezhi groups around the 1st century CE and expanded through Kabul, Gandhara and Taxila. His coins overstruck or imitated Indo-Greek issues of Hermaeus while adding Kharoshthi legends, a political language that turned borrowed symbols into Kushan legitimacy. RECENT FINDINGS: numismatic die studies separated the unnamed Soter Megas series from Kujula and linked it more securely to Vima Taktu. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Kujula a Buddhist patron like Kanishka; do NOT claim precise dates or a proven age of eighty-plus as fact.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Vima Kadphises Strikes the Gold Dinar
episodes.era: Kushan gold coinage and Mathura expansion, c. 100-127 CE
episodes.region: Mathura, Purushapura, Kapisa and the Indo-Roman trade routes
episodes.logline: Vima Kadphises mints heavy gold coins on a Roman-scale standard, turning Kushan power into money that could travel between four worlds.
episodes.moral: Trust is the hidden metal inside every coin.

sources.citation: Mathura statue inscription of Vima Kadphises, published in D.C. Sircar, Indian Epigraphy (1965)
sources.note: Primary evidence for Vima's royal titles and Mathura presence.

sources.citation: David Jongeward, Joe Cribb and Peter Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (ANS, 2015)
sources.note: Recent catalogue of Kushan coin weights, types and sequences.

sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.26 and 12.41
sources.note: Roman complaint about gold flowing east for Indian and Asian luxuries.

episodes.notes: Vima Kadphises issued Kushan gold coins of roughly 7.8-8.0 grams, near the Roman aureus standard, in an age when Roman bullion moved east for spices, textiles and silk. His coins show him at a fire altar and often carry Shiva with Nandi, while his Mathura statue presents a Central Asian ruler in boots and coat inside an Indian political landscape. RECENT FINDINGS: Jongeward-Cribb-Donovan and Robert Bracey's die studies refine the ruler sequence and coin chronology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call him the first Indian ruler ever to use gold; his innovation was standardized imperial gold coinage, not the invention of gold money. Do NOT invent direct Roman embassies.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: The Locked Rooms of Begram
episodes.era: Kushan trade at Kapisa, objects mainly 1st-2nd century CE
episodes.region: Begram or ancient Kapisa, Afghanistan
episodes.logline: Behind sealed mud-brick walls at Begram, Roman glass, Chinese lacquer and Indian ivories reveal the Kushans as brokers of the ancient world's busiest roads.
episodes.moral: Civilizations meet most quietly in the hands of traders and makers.

sources.citation: J. Hackin et al., Nouvelles recherches archeologiques a Begram (1954)
sources.note: Primary DAFA excavation publication for Rooms 10 and 13 and their objects.

sources.citation: Periplus Maris Erythraei, trans. Lionel Casson (1989)
sources.note: Contemporary merchant handbook for Indian Ocean routes linked to Kushan-era trade.

sources.citation: Roberta Tomber, Indo-Roman Trade (2008); Matthew Cobb, Rome and the Indian Ocean Trade (2018)
sources.note: Recent studies of the Roman and Indian Ocean sides of the exchange network.

episodes.notes: The Begram hoard, excavated by Joseph Hackin's DAFA team in 1936-40, contained Roman and Alexandrian glass, Egyptian bronzes, Han Chinese lacquer and more than a thousand Indian-style ivory and bone inlays. It shows Kapisa as a trade and storage hub at the meeting of the overland Silk Road, the Hindu Kush passes and Indian Ocean routes. RECENT FINDINGS: recovered and conserved Begram pieces since 2004 and Bertille Lyonnet's 2012 critique have complicated the old idea of one simple 1st-2nd century sealing event. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Kushans sailed to Rome; do NOT treat the hoard as a simple royal treasure without noting warehouse, gift-store and dating debates.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Kanishka's Sword on the Silk Road
episodes.era: Reign of Kanishka I, c. 127-150 CE by Falk's dating
episodes.region: Purushapura, Mathura, Kashmir, the Tarim Basin and the Gangetic plain
episodes.logline: Kanishka rules from Peshawar toward Central Asia and the Ganges, stamping coins as King of Kings while the Silk Road bends around his armies.
episodes.moral: Power is widest when it protects the roads it conquers.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, Cribb and Sims-Williams, JONS 160 (1995/96); revised by Sims-Williams (2008)
sources.note: Primary Bactrian evidence for Kanishka's genealogy and claimed eastern cities.

sources.citation: Hou Hanshu chapters 47 and 88, trans. John Hill (2009)
sources.note: Chinese record of Kushan-Han conflict and Central Asian context.

sources.citation: Harry Falk, The Yuga of Sphujiddhvaja and the Era of the Kushans, Silk Road Art and Archaeology 7 (2001)
sources.note: Influential argument for 127 CE as Year 1 of the Kanishka era.

episodes.notes: Kanishka I, probably beginning in 127 CE under Falk's widely used chronology, made Purushapura the main capital and claimed rule from Sindh to Saketa, Kausambi, Pataliputra and Sri-Champa in the Rabatak inscription. Chinese sources preserve a Kushan-Han conflict across the high routes into the Tarim Basin, though battle details remain Chinese court narrative rather than Kushan testimony. RECENT FINDINGS: the Rabatak inscription, found in 1993 and published in 1995/96, transformed understanding of Kushan geography; Cribb's coin studies separated Kanishka I from later Kanishkas. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say he certainly conquered or destroyed Pataliputra; Rabatak proves claimed rule or submission, not the exact military method.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Kanishka Raises the Sky Stupa
episodes.era: Kanishka's Buddhist monuments, c. 127-150 CE; excavated 1908-09
episodes.region: Shah-ji-Dheri near Peshawar and Surkh Kotal in Afghanistan
episodes.logline: At Purushapura, Kanishka's builders raise a gigantic stupa whose relic casket, pilgrim memories and ruined base still point upward.
episodes.moral: Great monuments should lift memory, not inflate pride.

sources.citation: D.B. Spooner, Excavations at Shah-ji-Dheri, Annual Report ASI 1908-09 (1912)
sources.note: Primary excavation report for the stupa base and Kanishka Casket context.

sources.citation: Faxian, Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms; Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions
sources.note: Chinese pilgrim descriptions of the Peshawar stupa centuries after Kanishka.

sources.citation: Kanishka Casket inscription; Surkh Kotal inscriptions, revised by Nicholas Sims-Williams (2012)
sources.note: Primary epigraphic evidence for patronage and Kushan building culture.

episodes.notes: At Shah-ji-Dheri near Peshawar, Spooner's excavations uncovered a massive cruciform base about 83 meters wide and the Kanishka Casket, a Kharoshthi-inscribed relic container associated with Sarvastivadin teachers. Faxian and Xuanzang later described an extraordinary stupa, but their height figures are probably exaggerated; modern estimates still make it one of ancient Asia's most ambitious Buddhist structures. RECENT FINDINGS: re-readings corrected the old Greek-name Agesilaos reading on the casket, while Surkh Kotal still preserves evidence of Kushan monumental architecture and a named architect Palamedes. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the stupa still stands; do NOT call it the tallest building in the ancient world.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: The Council Tradition in Kashmir
episodes.era: Northern Buddhist memory of Kanishka's council, c. 2nd century CE tradition
episodes.region: Kashmir, Gandhara and later Chinese Buddhist libraries
episodes.logline: In northern Buddhist memory, scholars gather under Kanishka to systematize the Dharma, but history asks which parts are text, tradition and legend.
episodes.moral: Wisdom grows stronger when honest doubt guards it.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, trans. Samuel Beal (1884)
sources.note: Later Chinese pilgrim account of Kanishka's council tradition.

sources.citation: Mahavibhasha, Chinese translation by Xuanzang, Taisho 1545
sources.note: Massive Sarvastivada commentary associated with the northwestern scholastic tradition.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999); Mark Allon et al., Gandhari Manuscripts: The Senior Collection (2007-)
sources.note: Recent manuscript publications showing Kushan-era Buddhist textual culture.

episodes.notes: The Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka is preserved in northern Sanskrit and Chinese Buddhist traditions, usually placed in Kashmir with Vasumitra, Parsva and sometimes Ashvaghosha among the learned figures. The Mahavibhasha and Sarvastivada scholastic culture are real, and the British Library and Senior Gandharan manuscripts provide physical evidence of 1st-2nd century Buddhist textual activity in the Kushan world. RECENT FINDINGS: the Gandharan birchbark scrolls acquired and published since 1994 revolutionized the evidence base but do not directly prove the council. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present the council, 500 monks or copper-plate storage as contemporary fact; Theravada tradition does not recognize this council.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: The First Human Face of the Buddha
episodes.era: Kushan-era Buddhist art, c. 1st-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Gandhara, Taxila, Peshawar, Swat and Mathura
episodes.logline: Under Kushan patronage, Gandhara and Mathura sculptors give the Buddha a human form that will travel across Asia in stone, stucco and faith.
episodes.moral: New beauty is often born where traditions meet without fear.

sources.citation: Inscribed Bala Bodhisattva and Kimbell Seated Bodhisattva, Kanishka-era Year 3 and Year 4
sources.note: Year-dated Mathura-school images anchoring the early Buddha image chronology.

sources.citation: John M. Rosenfield, The Dynastic Arts of the Kushans (1967)
sources.note: Foundational study of Kushan royal and religious art.

sources.citation: Robert DeCaroli, Image Problems: The Origin and Development of the Buddha's Image in Early South Asia (2015)
sources.note: Recent treatment of the aniconic-to-iconic transition and Gandhara-Mathura debate.

episodes.notes: Kushan-era patronage fostered two great image-making centers: Gandhara, with schist and stucco figures shaped by Hellenistic visual language, and Mathura, with red sandstone images growing from Indian yaksha traditions. The Bala Bodhisattva and Kimbell Bodhisattva have Kanishka-era inscriptions, making Mathura especially well dated, while Gandhara supplied forms that traveled widely into East Asia. RECENT FINDINGS: a Mathura-style red sandstone sculpture found at Taxila in 2008 suggests stronger exchange between the two schools than older models allowed. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Greeks invented Buddhist art; do NOT claim Gandhara definitely preceded Mathura, because the primacy debate remains unresolved.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: Ashvaghosha Sings the Buddha's Life
episodes.region: Saketa, Purushapura and the Silk Road manuscript world
episodes.logline: Ashvaghosha turns Buddhist teaching into polished Sanskrit poetry whose words move from Kushan monasteries toward China and Tibet.
episodes.moral: A story can carry philosophy farther than argument alone.

sources.citation: Ashvaghosha, Buddhacharita and Saundarananda, ed. E.H. Johnston (1936)
sources.note: Surviving Sanskrit works and translations attributed to the Kushan-era poet.

sources.citation: Chinese Biography of Ashvaghosha, attributed to Kumarajiva's translation, c. 402-409 CE
sources.note: Later source for legendary court and conversion stories.

sources.citation: Patrick Olivelle, Life of the Buddha by Ashvaghosha (2008); Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999)
sources.note: Modern translation and manuscript context for Kushan Buddhist literature.

episodes.notes: Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita and Saundarananda show the Kushan age as a scholarly and literary crossroads, using sophisticated Sanskrit kavya to tell Buddhist lives and ideals. Turfan fragments of Shariputraprakarana may preserve early Sanskrit drama associated with him, and his works survived through Chinese and Tibetan transmission along Silk Road networks. RECENT FINDINGS: continuing study of Gandharan, Turfan and Schoyen manuscript fragments refines the picture of Kushan textual culture. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat the starving horses moved to tears, his capture by Kanishka or his Brahmin conversion story as verified; they are later hagiography. Do NOT call him definitively India's first playwright.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: Thirty Gods on Kushan Coins
episodes.era: Kushan multi-faith coinage, c. 1st-2nd century CE
episodes.region: Bactria, Gandhara, Kapisa and Mathura
episodes.logline: Kushan coins place Iranian, Greek, Indian, Egyptian and Buddhist figures in one imperial language, making plural patronage visible in every marketplace.
episodes.moral: Respect grows when power learns the names of many gods.

sources.citation: Jongeward, Cribb and Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (2015)
sources.note: Catalogue documenting the extraordinary deity range on Kushan coinage.

sources.citation: Rabatak inscription, Cribb and Sims-Williams (1995/96)
sources.note: Kanishka's own Bactrian statement of kingship from Nana and all the gods.

sources.citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams, Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan (ongoing)
sources.note: Corpus clarifying Bactrian language and post-Kushan administrative culture.

episodes.notes: Kushan coins display more than thirty deities across traditions, including Nana, Miiro, Aurmuzd, Ardoxsho, Buddha, Oesho, Serapis and others, all named in Bactrian written with Greek letters. The Rabatak inscription says Kanishka received kingship from Nana and all the gods and ordered divine and royal images, making plural patronage part of state display. RECENT FINDINGS: the Oesho identification is debated, with some scholars seeing Vayu-Vata conflated with Shiva, and Bactrian-document studies keep refining the cultural map. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call this modern religious tolerance; it was strategic imperial patronage. Do NOT claim Kanishka converted exclusively to Buddhism.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Where Gods Met and Art Was Born

episodes.title: Huvishka's Amitabha in Mathura
episodes.era: Huvishka's reign and Mathura devotion, c. 150-190 CE
episodes.region: Mathura, Purushapura, Kapisa and Ayrtam
episodes.logline: In Huvishka's prosperous reign, a merchant family's Mathura inscription names Amitabha, hinting at a devotion that will one day fill East Asia.
episodes.moral: Small dedications can become long rivers of memory.

sources.citation: Govindo-Nagar Amitabha inscription, Mathura Museum, Year 28 of Huvishka
sources.note: Earliest known epigraphic reference to Amitabha Buddha.

sources.citation: Ayrtam inscription and Surkh Kotal SK4, published and revised by Harmatta and Sims-Williams
sources.note: Evidence for Huvishka-era cult and Bactrian inscriptional culture.

sources.citation: Paul Harrison, Who Gets to Ride in the Great Vehicle?, JIABS 10.1 (1987); Jongeward-Cribb-Donovan (2015)
sources.note: Scholarly work on Amitabha origins and Huvishka coinage.

episodes.notes: Huvishka ruled for about four decades and issued some of the most diverse Kushan coinage, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and even Egyptian deities such as Serapis. The Govindo-Nagar inscription from Mathura, dated Year 28 of Huvishka, dedicates a statue to Amitabha Buddha by a merchant family and is crucial for tracing early Mahayana and Pure Land devotion. RECENT FINDINGS: Schoyen and other manuscript studies connect Huvishka's era to wider Mahayana development, but do not prove his personal doctrine. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Huvishka founded Pure Land Buddhism; the inscription shows Amitabha devotion existed, not that later East Asian Pure Land systems were complete.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Vasudeva and the Long Unraveling
episodes.era: Late Great Kushan period, c. 191-232 CE and after
episodes.region: Mathura, Gandhara, Bactria and the Sasanian frontier
episodes.logline: As Vasudeva's coins turn toward Shiva and Nandi, Sasanian pressure in the west and new rivals in the east begin to pull the Kushan world apart.
episodes.moral: Decline is often a slow loosening, not a single fall.

sources.citation: Jongeward, Cribb and Donovan, Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian, and Kidarite Coins (2015)
sources.note: Coin sequence for Vasudeva, later Kushans and Kushano-Sasanians.

sources.citation: Shapur I, Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription, c. 262 CE, trans. M. Back (1978)
sources.note: Sasanian royal claim over Kushan territory or Kushanshar.

sources.citation: Khodadad Rezakhani, ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017)
sources.note: Recent study of East Iran, Kushano-Sasanian rule and late antique frontiers.

episodes.notes: Vasudeva I, often treated as the last Great Kushan, ruled as the empire's western holdings came under pressure from Ardashir I, Shapur I and later Kushano-Sasanian governors styling themselves Kushanshah. His coins strongly emphasize Shiva with Nandi, unlike the broader pantheons of Kanishka and Huvishka, while later eastern or Little Kushans persisted in reduced form until Gupta, Kidarite and other powers absorbed their territories. RECENT FINDINGS: newer numismatic work distinguishes Great Kushan, Kushano-Sasanian and Kidarite issues more carefully. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the empire simply fell to the Guptas; western loss to Sasanians and northern pressure were central, and the process was gradual.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Buddhism's Road to China
episodes.era: Silk Road Buddhist transmission, c. 148-400 CE
episodes.region: Gandhara, the Tarim Basin, Dunhuang and Luoyang
episodes.logline: Monks and merchants carry Gandharan manuscripts through Kushan roads to Luoyang, where Lokaraksha turns Mahayana ideas into Chinese words.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farthest when roads, books and seekers meet.

sources.citation: Lokaraksha's early Chinese Buddhist translations in the Taisho canon, identified by Erik Zurcher and Jan Nattier
sources.note: Primary textual evidence for Gandharan and Kushan-era transmission to China.

sources.citation: British Library Gandharan manuscripts, published by Richard Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999)
sources.note: Physical Kharoshthi birchbark evidence for early Buddhist scribal culture.

sources.citation: Faxian, Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, trans. James Legge (1886)
sources.note: Later pilgrim account of Buddhist landscapes that inherited Kushan-era networks.

episodes.notes: Lokaraksha, active at Luoyang around 148-170 CE and associated with Gandhara/Yuezhi background, produced some of the earliest Chinese Mahayana translations, while An Shigao and other translators worked in the same Han world. The Gandharan birchbark manuscripts, acquired and published from the 1990s onward, physically demonstrate the scribal culture from which such texts could travel through Tarim oasis monasteries to China. RECENT FINDINGS: Salomon's Gandhari manuscript project and Jan Nattier's work on earliest Chinese translations have made the Kushan-era transmission map far sharper. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Kanishka sent missionaries to China; evidence points to monks and merchants using protected trade routes. Do NOT say Buddhism began in China only with the Kushans.
episodes.chapter: The Kushan Empire and the Silk Road

episodes.title: Simhavishnu Ends the Kalabhra Night
episodes.era: Pallava revival, c. 555-600 CE, with dates debated
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tondaimandalam and the Kaveri frontier
episodes.logline: After a shadowed age in Tamil history, Simhavishnu restores Pallava power from Kanchipuram and turns the court toward conquest, Vishnu worship and Sanskrit learning.
episodes.moral: A revival begins by turning memory into disciplined action.

sources.citation: Udayendiram copper plates of Nandivarman II
sources.note: Retrospective Pallava record naming Simhavishnu, his Vaishnava affiliation and campaigns.

sources.citation: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II
sources.note: Full Pallava genealogy and eulogistic account of the dynasty's revival.

sources.citation: Rajan Gurukkal, Social Formations of Early South India (2010); K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (2008 reprint)
sources.note: Modern reassessment of the Kalabhra period and Pallava chronology.

episodes.notes: Simhavishnu, son of Simhavarman III, is the first imperial Pallava ruler whose power clearly reached beyond Kanchipuram, probably extending south toward the Kaveri and challenging Pandyas and Lanka-linked powers. The evidence is mostly retrospective copper plates, not inscriptions issued by Simhavishnu himself, and scholarly dates range roughly from the mid-6th to early 7th century. KEY RECENT FINDING: modern scholars such as Rajan Gurukkal warn that the Kalabhra 'dark age' was partly a later Brahmanical and dynastic framing; do NOT portray the whole period as cultural collapse. Do NOT state the legendary Ashwatthama or Naga ancestry in Pallava plates as fact.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: I. Kanchi Rises from the Kalabhra Haze

episodes.title: Mahendravarman's Vow Without Mortar
episodes.region: Mandagapattu, Mamandur, Kudimiyamalai and Kanchipuram
episodes.logline: A king who writes farce, studies music and cuts shrines from living rock declares that his new temple will use no brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal.
episodes.moral: Innovation begins when imagination refuses old limits.

sources.citation: Mandagapattu Tirumurti temple inscription of Mahendravarman I
sources.note: Primary rock inscription proclaiming a shrine made without brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal.

sources.citation: Kudimiyamalai music inscription, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II, No. 68
sources.note: Early musicological inscription associated with Mahendravarman's courtly world.

sources.citation: Mahendravarman I, Mattavilasa Prahasana, ed. M. Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat (1981)
sources.note: Sanskrit farce set in Kanchipuram and reflecting its religious plurality.

episodes.notes: Mahendravarman I was a warrior, artist, playwright and temple innovator. His Mandagapattu inscription is the famous engineering claim that the temple was made without brick, wood, lime, mortar or metal, marking the Pallava rock-cut turn; his Mamandur inscription connects him with plays, while the Kudimiyamalai inscription preserves rare early music theory. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Marilyn Hirsh and R. Champakalakshmi stress the king's creative patronage while warning that his Jain-to-Shaiva 'conversion' is better read as a shift in patronage, not a simple doctrinal drama. Do NOT attribute all Mamallapuram monuments to him, and do NOT retell Periya Puranam miracles as biography.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: I. Kanchi Rises from the Kalabhra Haze

episodes.title: Mamalla Takes Vatapi
episodes.era: Pallava-Chalukya war and Vatapi campaign, c. 630-654 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Manimangalam and Vatapi (Badami)
episodes.logline: Narasimhavarman Mamalla answers his father's defeat by driving north, taking Vatapi in 642 CE, and turning a Chalukya boast into a Pallava legend.
episodes.moral: A setback can become strength when patience waits for the right hour.

sources.citation: Kuram copper-plate grant of Paramesvaravarman I, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I
sources.note: Pallava account of victories over Pulakeshin and the destruction of Vatapi.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyuji, Book X, on Kanchipuram c. 640 CE
sources.note: Eyewitness account of Kanchi's religious institutions and prosperity during Mamalla's reign.

sources.citation: Culavamsa, chapters 41-44
sources.note: Sri Lankan record of Manavarman's Pallava alliance and Narasimhavarman's Lanka expeditions.

episodes.notes: Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla or Great Wrestler, defeated Chalukya forces near Kanchi and sent Paranjothi north to capture Vatapi in 642 CE; Pallava forces likely held the city until the Chalukya recovery around 654 CE. Xuanzang's visit around 640 CE gives an independent portrait of a prosperous Kanchipuram with Buddhist monasteries and Hindu temples. RECENT DEBATE: the Chalukya record gap after 642 strongly suggests Pulakeshin II died in the crisis, but no Chalukya inscription says exactly how. Do NOT state with certainty that Pulakeshin died in a named duel or that miracle stories from later hagiography caused the victory.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: II. Wrestlers, Exiles and Crowned Boys

episodes.title: The Boy from Kambuja Crowned at Kanchi
episodes.era: Pallava succession crisis and reign, c. 731-796 CE
episodes.region: Kambujadesa, Kanchipuram and the Vaikunta Perumal temple
episodes.logline: When the royal line falters, Pallava ministers find a twelve-year-old collateral prince across the sea and crown him in Kanchipuram as Nandivarman II.
episodes.moral: Legitimacy survives when a community can renew its institutions.

sources.citation: Kasakudi copper plates of Nandivarman II, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. II
sources.note: Primary record for the succession narrative and Pallava genealogy.

sources.citation: Vaikunta Perumal temple relief panels, Kanchipuram
sources.note: Visual dynastic narrative showing the search for and coronation of Nandivarman II.

sources.citation: D. Dennis Hudson, The Body of God (2008)
sources.note: Detailed modern study of the Vaikunta Perumal temple as royal and religious narrative.

episodes.notes: After Paramesvaravarman II died without an heir, Pallava elites selected the young Pallavamalla from a collateral line associated in the plates with Kambujadesa and crowned him Nandivarman II. The Vaikunta Perumal temple's cloister panels turn this crisis into one of India's rare early dynastic autobiographies in stone. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Dennis Hudson dates and interprets the temple as both a palace of Krishna and a political monument. Do NOT claim the precise Kambujadesa location is certain, and do NOT accept the 54-king divine genealogy from Brahma and Ashwatthama as history.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: II. Wrestlers, Exiles and Crowned Boys

episodes.title: Five Generations Across the Deccan
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Pullalur, Manimangalam, Vatapi and the Deccan routes
episodes.logline: Across more than a century, Pallava and Chalukya courts turn the same battles into rival poems of humiliation, revenge, endurance and royal glory.
episodes.moral: History is clearest when rival voices are heard together.

sources.citation: Aihole prashasti of Pulakeshin II by Ravikirti, Saka 556 / c. 634 CE
sources.note: Chalukya victory narrative for the Pullalur campaign against Mahendravarman I.

sources.citation: Kuram copper plates and Velurpalaiyam plates of the Pallavas
sources.note: Pallava counter-narratives for the Vatapi revenge and later victories.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (2001); Hermann Kulke and Dietmar Rothermund, A History of India (2004)
sources.note: Modern framing of inscriptional war narratives and temple-state politics.

episodes.notes: The Pallava-Chalukya struggle began with Pulakeshin II's victory over Mahendravarman I near Pullalur around 618-619 CE, peaked with Narasimhavarman I's capture of Vatapi in 642 CE, and continued through Chalukya occupation threats and Nandivarman II's recovery with Rashtrakuta help. The Aihole prashasti and Pallava plates are political poems, not neutral reports. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats these inscriptions as performances of legitimacy. Do NOT present either side's metaphors, such as writing victory on an enemy's back, as literal battlefield journalism; and do NOT duplicate the Chalukya point of view without showing Pallava endurance.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Paranjothi Carries Home Vatapi Ganapati
episodes.era: Vatapi campaign and Nayanar memory, c. 642 CE and later
episodes.region: Vatapi, Kanchipuram and Tiruchengattankudy
episodes.logline: The general Paranjothi returns from Vatapi with victory spoils and later memory transforms him into Siruthondar, a warrior among the Shaiva saints.
episodes.moral: Service can change its form without losing its discipline.

sources.citation: Kuram copper plates of the Pallavas
sources.note: Epigraphic basis for the Vatapi campaign and Paranjothi's military context.

sources.citation: Sundarar, Tiruthonda Thogai
sources.note: Earliest canonical list of Nayanmars, including Siruthondar before later full legends.

sources.citation: Indira Viswanathan Peterson, Poems to Siva (1989); Norman Cutler, Songs of Experience (1987)
sources.note: Modern scholarship distinguishing Bhakti hymns from later hagiography.

episodes.notes: Paranjothi, traditionally linked with the title Vikrama Kesari, is remembered as Narasimhavarman I's commander in the Vatapi campaign and as Siruthondar among the 63 Nayanmars. The Vatapi Ganapati tradition at Tiruchengattankudy preserves the idea of a religious trophy brought from the defeated Chalukya capital. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: the identification of Paranjothi the general with Siruthondar is traditional, not epigraphically proven; the child-sacrifice test in the Periya Puranam is a 12th-century hagiographic legend and must not be narrated as fact. The useful historical point is the social breadth of Bhakti, where warriors, farmers, merchants, women and marginalized devotees all enter sacred memory.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Mamallapuram's Stone Theater
episodes.era: Mamallapuram monuments, c. 630-728 CE, with later discoveries in 2004-2005
episodes.region: Mamallapuram on the Coromandel Coast
episodes.logline: Granite outcrops become chariot temples, ocean shrines and a vast carved cliff where water may once have made the Ganga descend before festival crowds.
episodes.moral: Great art teaches stone to move.

sources.citation: UNESCO, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram World Heritage nomination (1984)
sources.note: Heritage documentation for the monument group.

sources.citation: Shore Temple inscriptions naming Kshatriyasimha and Rajasimha Pallavesvara shrines
sources.note: Primary epigraphic basis for Rajasimha-period structural works.

sources.citation: NIOT/ASI Underwater Exploration off Mahabalipuram Coast, interim reports 2005
sources.note: Post-tsunami documentation of submerged structures linked cautiously to the Seven Pagodas tradition.

episodes.notes: Mamallapuram's Pancha Rathas, cave shrines, Descent of the Ganges or Arjuna's Penance relief, and Shore Temple span multiple Pallava reigns from Mamalla to Rajasimha. The great relief may have used a water channel in its central cleft, making sculpture, myth and hydraulic theater work together. RECENT FINDING: after the 2004 tsunami, NIOT and ASI surveys documented submerged stone structures offshore, supporting but not proving the Seven Pagodas tradition. Do NOT attribute the entire site to one king, and do NOT claim the underwater remains are fully dated Pallava temples until publication confirms it.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: Rajasimha Builds the Kailasanathar
episodes.region: Kanchipuram and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram
episodes.logline: Rajasimha turns Pallava experiment into structural stone, raising Kailasanathar as a royal shrine, icon gallery and prototype for South Indian temple building.
episodes.moral: A lasting tradition begins as someone's bold experiment.

sources.citation: Kailasanathar temple inscriptions, South Indian Inscriptions, Vol. I and later epigraphic editions
sources.note: Primary evidence naming Rajasimha's shrine and royal builders.

sources.citation: ASI conservation and mural documentation at Kailasanathar temple, Kanchipuram
sources.note: Material evidence for architecture, paintings and conservation history.

sources.citation: Padma Kaimal, studies of the Kailasanathar temple and Pallava art, 1990s-2010s
sources.note: Modern architectural and iconographic reassessment.

episodes.notes: The Kailasanathar temple, begun by Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha and completed or expanded by his son, uses granite foundations and carved sandstone superstructure, with subsidiary shrines and a wall of Shaiva iconography that influenced later Dravidian temples. Its old murals connect Pallava Kanchi to wider Indian painting traditions. RECENT DOCUMENTATION has refined the temple's c. 700-728 CE date and recorded fragile paintings. Do NOT claim with certainty that Rajaraja Chola personally copied it for Brihadisvara, though later Chola architecture clearly inherited Pallava structural experiments; and do NOT present popular tunnel stories as archaeology.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: The Pallava Alphabet Goes Overseas
episodes.era: Pallava script diffusion, c. 5th-9th centuries CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, the Coromandel Coast, Cambodia, Java, Champa and Burma
episodes.logline: A courtly script shaped for Sanskrit and Tamil travels with priests, traders and diplomats until it becomes an ancestor of writing systems across Southeast Asia.
episodes.moral: Ideas travel farther when people give them durable signs.

sources.citation: Pallava inscriptions at Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram compared with early Khmer, Cham, Malay and Javanese inscriptions
sources.note: Epigraphic basis for tracing Pallava-derived scripts.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (2006)
sources.note: Framework for Sanskrit cosmopolis and script-cultural transmission.

sources.citation: Anshuman Pandey, Proposal to Encode the Pallava Script in Unicode, L2/18-084 (2018)
sources.note: Modern palaeographic and computational documentation of Pallava script forms.

episodes.notes: Pallava-Grantha writing carried Sanskrit prestige and local administrative practice into Southeast Asian courts, helping shape Old Khmer, Cham, Kawi, Old Malay, Mon and later regional scripts, while also influencing Malayalam and southern Indian script histories. RECENT EFEO epigraphic work and digital palaeography continue to map regional variants and routes. Do NOT claim one named Pallava king personally invented every Southeast Asian script; the transmission mechanism involved merchants, monks, Brahmins and courts over centuries. This is a scholarly innovation story about writing systems, not a conquest story.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Stone, Script and the Sea

episodes.title: Copper Plates and Village Sabhas
episodes.era: Pallava land grants and local institutions, c. 4th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tondaimandalam and brahmadeya villages
episodes.logline: Thin copper sheets record how kings, Brahmin settlements, irrigation rights and village sabhas reshaped land, learning and local power.
episodes.moral: Institutions endure when written promises meet local responsibility.

sources.citation: Mayidavolu and Hirahadagalli copper plates of Sivaskandavarman, Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XV
sources.note: Early Prakrit Pallava grants showing Satavahana-era administrative inheritance.

sources.citation: Kasakudi, Udayendiram and Tandantottam copper plates
sources.note: Bilingual Sanskrit-Tamil grants with genealogy, boundaries, taxes and local administration.

sources.citation: R. Champakalakshmi, Trade and Urban Centres in Early Historic South India (1996); R.S. Sharma, Indian Feudalism, 3rd ed. (2001)
sources.note: Contrasting interpretations of brahmadeya grants as development and power transfer.

episodes.notes: Pallava copper plates show royal grants, land boundaries, tax exemptions, irrigation rights and the growth of brahmadeya villages administered by sabhas of Brahmin landholders. Kanchipuram also appears as a ghatikasthana, a center of learning, while Xuanzang describes a plural city with Buddhist and Hindu institutions. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP debates whether these grants developed agriculture and learning or also displaced older cultivators and concentrated power. Do NOT describe the sabha as modern democracy; it was a restricted local institution, important but socially bounded. Do NOT repeat Chola Uttaramerur details as if they were already fully Pallava.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Mariners of Mamallapuram
episodes.era: Pallava port trade and diplomacy, c. 7th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Mamallapuram, Nagapattinam, Sri Lanka, Tang China and the Bay of Bengal
episodes.logline: Ships at Mamallapuram carry gems, elephants, envoys, monks and scripts across the Bay of Bengal, tying Pallava Kanchi to Lanka, China and Southeast Asia.
episodes.moral: Prosperity grows when shores become meeting places.

sources.citation: Thirumangai Alvar, Periya Tirumoli
sources.note: 8th-century Tamil hymn vividly describing ships and wealth at Mamallapuram.

sources.citation: Tang Annals (Tangshu) on the Pallava embassy of c. 720 CE
sources.note: Chinese record of Rajasimha's diplomatic contact with Tang Xuanzong.

sources.citation: Kanakalatha Mukund, The World of Tamil Merchants (2015); Pierre-Yves Manguin et al., Early Interactions between South and Southeast Asia (2011)
sources.note: Modern studies of Tamil merchant and Bay of Bengal networks.

episodes.notes: Mamallapuram was a Pallava port distinct from inland Kanchipuram. Literary testimony, coins, maritime diplomacy, Sri Lankan chronicle material and Tang records connect the Pallavas to Sri Lanka, China and Southeast Asia; Rajasimha's embassy to Tang China and the remembered China Pagoda at Nagapattinam show Buddhist and diplomatic dimensions. RECENT WORK by Mukund, Manguin and Ranabir Chakravarti places the port in wider Bay of Bengal economic systems. Do NOT overstate the scale of trade from isolated coin finds, and do NOT treat the Tang honorific as proof that Rajasimha commanded Chinese armies.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Appar Sings the King Toward Siva
episodes.era: Early Tamil Shaiva Bhakti, c. 600-650 CE
episodes.region: Kanchipuram, Tiruvathigai and Pallava Tamil country
episodes.logline: Appar's Tamil hymns carry devotion beyond elite ritual and later memory links his songs to Mahendravarman's turn from Jain patronage toward Siva.
episodes.moral: A song in the people's language can change public life.

sources.citation: Appar's Tevaram hymns, Tirumurai volumes 4-6
sources.note: Primary devotional corpus for Appar's voice and religious world.

sources.citation: Mandagapattu inscription of Mahendravarman I
sources.note: Royal Shaiva temple dedication consistent with a shift in patronage.

sources.citation: Indira Viswanathan Peterson, Poems to Siva (1989); Karen Pechilis, The Embodiment of Bhakti (1999)
sources.note: Modern scholarship on Bhakti sources, embodiment and social scope.

episodes.notes: Appar, a Vellalar devotee remembered as once Jain, composed Tamil hymns that helped make temple devotion emotionally direct and publicly performable. Later hagiography says he converted Mahendravarman I from Jainism to Shaivism; inscriptions instead show a religious shift in the king's patronage, not the dramatic prison-and-miracle story. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP emphasizes the hymns themselves over Periya Puranam biography and debates how far Bhakti should be called social reform. Do NOT say Bhakti abolished caste or that the king became intolerant; the Pallava religious landscape remained plural, with Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical institutions present.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: Women Who Sang the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.era: Women poet-saints of Tamil Bhakti, c. 5th-8th centuries CE
episodes.region: Karaikal, Thiruvalangadu, Srivilliputhur and the wider Tamil country
episodes.logline: Karaikkal Ammaiyar and Andal turn Tamil poetry into a woman's devotional voice, from cremation-ground Siva songs to Krishna longing sung every Margazhi.
episodes.moral: A tradition is richer when every voice can sing.

sources.citation: Karaikkal Ammaiyar's Arpudath Thiruvandhadhi and Thiruvaalangadu hymns, 11th Tirumurai
sources.note: Primary Shaiva poems attributed to one of the earliest women Nayanmars.

sources.citation: Andal's Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli, Naalayira Divya Prabandham
sources.note: Primary Vaishnava poems of the only woman Alvar.

sources.citation: Elaine Craddock, Siva's Demon Devotee (2010); Archana Venkatesan, The Secret Garland (2010)
sources.note: Recent critical studies separating poetry from later miracle biographies.

episodes.notes: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, probably among the earliest Nayanmars, used fierce poetic images of Shiva's cremation-ground dance and helped shape Tamil devotional form; Andal, active around the 8th century in most scholarly dating, composed the Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli in a female voice of vow, longing and theology. RECENT STUDIES by Craddock and Venkatesan foreground their literary agency and distinguish primary poems from later hagiographies. Do NOT claim exact dates are certain, do NOT treat Andal's miraculous union with Ranganatha or Ammaiyar's bodily transformation as contemporary fact, and do NOT erase their different Shaiva and Vaishnava contexts.
episodes.chapter: The Pallavas and the Bhakti Dawn
episodes.chapter_part: V. Villages, Voices and the Bhakti Dawn

episodes.title: The River That Taught the Stars
episodes.region: The Nila or Bharathappuzha valley, Tirunavaya, Tirur and Ponnani, Kerala
episodes.logline: Along the Nila River, memorized number-verses, almanacs and scholar-houses prepared the ground for Kerala's later leap toward infinity.
episodes.moral: Great discoveries grow from patient traditions.

sources.citation: Haridatta, Grahacara-nibandhana, c. 683 CE
sources.note: Early Kerala astronomical text using the Katapayadi numeral system and the Parahita computation tradition.

sources.citation: Govinda Bhattathiri, Muhurtaratnam; Paramesvara's commentary on it
sources.note: Lineage evidence linking later Kerala astronomers to an older Nila-valley tradition.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972); Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
sources.note: Modern reconstruction of the early Kerala lineage and its mnemonic techniques.

episodes.notes: Start before Madhava. Haridatta's Parahita system, dated by its 683 CE epoch, and the Katapayadi system show a local technology for turning numbers into memorable syllables. Govinda Bhattathiri represents the later astrological-astronomical tradition that Paramesvara says his own family inherited. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Sarma's lineage remains the standard framework, but many personal details come from internal textual references, not inscriptions. Do NOT treat folklore from Ithihyamala as documentary biography, and do NOT pretend the Kerala school appeared suddenly from nowhere.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Country of the River

episodes.title: Madhava at the House of the Ilanchi Tree
episodes.era: Founding generation of the Kerala school, c. 1340-c. 1425
episodes.region: Sangamagrama, probably Kudallur near the Nila-Kunti confluence, Kerala
episodes.logline: From a small river settlement, Madhava becomes the remembered founder whose followers credit him with series that reached beyond the mathematics of his age.
episodes.moral: A quiet village can change the world's questions.

sources.citation: Madhava, Venvaroha, 1403 CE, ed. K.V. Sarma (1956)
sources.note: Dated surviving astronomical work establishing Madhava's historical identity.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Tantrasangraha, 1500-1501; Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550
sources.note: Later Kerala texts repeatedly attribute the infinite series tradition to Madhava.

sources.citation: P.P. Divakaran, The Mathematics of India (2018); C.T. Rajagopal and M.S. Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978)
sources.note: Recent and classic analysis of Madhava's location, methods and attributed verses.

episodes.notes: Madhava's biography is a sources problem: no contemporary inscription records his birth or death, and his famous mathematical series survive through later attributions rather than autograph proof-texts. His surviving works such as Venvaroha and Sphutacandrapti are astronomical. Divakaran favors Kudallur near the Nila-Kunti confluence over the popular Irinjalakuda identification; present the location as probable, not certain. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT call Madhava the inventor of calculus or sole author of all later Kerala mathematics; say his school preserved reliable attributions to him for specific infinite series used in astronomy.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Country of the River

episodes.title: Paramesvara Watches Fifty Five Years
episodes.era: Drigganita reform and observational astronomy, c. 1393-1443
episodes.region: Alathiyur and the Nila valley, Kerala
episodes.logline: Refusing to trust old tables blindly, Paramesvara compares eclipses with the sky for decades and rebuilds computation around observation.
episodes.moral: Truth improves when tradition listens to evidence.

sources.citation: Paramesvara, Drigganita, 1431 CE; Grahanamandana, epoch 1411 CE; Goladipika, 1443 CE
sources.note: Primary texts for the observation-based correction program.

sources.citation: David Pingree, Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit, Series A vol. 4 (1981)
sources.note: Manuscript census listing Paramesvara's large surviving corpus.

sources.citation: K. Ramasubramanian, M.D. Srinivas and M.S. Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Modern account of Kerala model modifications beginning with Paramesvara.

episodes.notes: Paramesvara, the confirmed direct pupil of Madhava, belonged to the Vatasseri family at Alathiyur. His Drigganita, literally sight-computation, corrected the older Parahita constants through eclipse observation and helped shape Kerala almanac practice. KEY FACTS: Grahanamandana uses a 1411 epoch, Drigganita was completed in 1431, and Goladipika in 1443; the often-cited 55-year span is inferred from text dates and observation references. Do NOT claim modern laboratory science, but do highlight the unusually explicit empirical correction tradition and his cyclic-quadrilateral circumradius result later seen in Europe with Lhuilier.

episodes.title: Nilakantha Moves the Planets Around the Sun
episodes.region: Trikkandiyur, Kelallur Illam and Kerala's scholarly network
episodes.logline: Nilakantha keeps Earth at the center of the cosmos but lets the planets circle the Sun, creating a model mathematically close to Tycho's before Tycho.
episodes.moral: Innovation can revise a tradition from within.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Tantrasangraha, completed 1500-1501 CE
sources.note: Precisely dated Sanskrit synthesis of planetary theory, spherical astronomy and series results.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Aryabhatiya-bhasya and Jyotirmimamsa, ed. K.V. Sarma
sources.note: Primary sources for his revised planetary model and observational method.

sources.citation: Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); K.V. Sarma and K. Ramasubramanian, Tantrasangraha translation (2011)
sources.note: Modern interpretation of the geo-heliocentric model and full translation of the text.

episodes.notes: Nilakantha is unusually well dated: his own Siddhanta-darpana gives Kali-day 1,660,181, converted to 14 June 1444. Tantrasangraha has internal chronograms for 1500-1501 and 432 verses in eight chapters. RECENT FINDING: the 1994 Current Science paper made the strongest case that his model places Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn around the Sun while the Sun circles Earth, a Tychonic-equivalent geometry. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT call him a full heliocentrist or a Copernicus before Copernicus; he retained a geocentric cosmology while transforming the mathematical model.

episodes.title: The Series That Reached Pi
episodes.region: Kerala manuscripts of Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasa and Yukti-dipika
episodes.logline: Kerala mathematicians express pi, sine, cosine and arctangent as endless series, then add error terms that make infinity useful.
episodes.moral: The infinite becomes powerful when it is made precise.

sources.citation: Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, c. 1530-1550, tr. K.V. Sarma et al. as Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa (2008)
sources.note: Malayalam proof-text giving derivations of the pi and trigonometric series.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Yukti-dipika, verses on Madhava's sine series and Katapayadi pi value
sources.note: Preserves quoted Sanskrit verses attributed to Madhava.

sources.citation: Victor J. Katz, Mathematics Magazine 68:3 (1995); David Bressoud, College Mathematics Journal 33:1 (2002); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Careful modern framing of Kerala series as precursors, not full calculus.

episodes.notes: This is the core mathematical innovation story. The school knew the alternating pi over four series, arctangent series, sine and cosine series, and correction terms that made approximations fast enough to be practical; a Katapayadi verse preserved pi to 11 decimal places. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: historians now distinguish components of calculus from calculus as a unified theory. Do NOT say Kerala invented calculus, and do NOT imply Madhava had the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, general functions, or Newton-Leibniz notation. The correct claim is stronger and cleaner: specific infinite series appeared in Kerala roughly two to three centuries before their European rediscovery.

episodes.title: Jyeshthadeva Writes Proofs in Malayalam
episodes.region: Parangngottu family area near Trikkandiyur and Tirur, Kerala
episodes.logline: Jyeshthadeva turns difficult Sanskrit astronomy into Malayalam reasoning, preserving proofs of the series in a language students could follow.
episodes.moral: Knowledge travels farther when proof is made speakable.

sources.citation: Jyeshthadeva, Yuktibhasa, tr. K.V. Sarma, K. Ramasubramanian, M.D. Srinivas and M.S. Sriram, Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa (Springer, 2008)
sources.note: Complete English translation of the Malayalam proof-text.

sources.citation: Acyuta Pisharati, Uparagakriyakrama, 1592 CE
sources.note: Mentions Jyeshthadeva as an aged teacher and helps anchor his chronology.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 237-248; K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School (1972)
sources.note: Modern analysis of the text's proof structure and dating.

episodes.notes: Yuktibhasa is one of the world's most remarkable vernacular mathematical works: it gives extended explanations and proofs for results that many Sanskrit texts state in compressed verse. It covers arithmetic, geometry, spherical astronomy, eclipses, planetary computation and the Madhava series. ACCURACY FLAGS: c. 1530 is an inferred date, with some scholars preferring a wider c. 1530-1550 range; no extant manuscript colophon fixes the composition date. Do NOT exaggerate by calling it the first proof text in the world, but it is safely framed as the earliest known extended mathematical proof-text in an Indian vernacular.

episodes.title: Sankara Variyar Saves the Verses
episodes.region: Kerala temple-service and scholarly communities
episodes.logline: A temple-service scholar comments line by line until Madhava's most fragile verses survive inside the margins of another book.
episodes.moral: Preservation is also a form of genius.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Yukti-dipika or Tantrasamgraha-vyakhya
sources.note: Commentary preserving Madhava's quoted series verses and Nilakantha's text.

sources.citation: Sankara Variyar, Kriyakramakarini, ed. K.V. Sarma and S. Hariharan (1975)
sources.note: Commentary on Bhaskara II's Lilavati showing his broader mathematical learning.

sources.citation: C.T. Rajagopal and T.V. Vedamurti, Scripta Mathematica 17 (1951); Rajagopal and Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978)
sources.note: Modern recovery of the Sanskrit series material.

episodes.notes: Sankara Variyar was not a Nambudiri but a Variyar, from a temple-service community, which complicates any simple caste-only picture of the school. His Yukti-dipika is vital because it preserves verses explicitly attributed to Madhava, including the sine series and the Katapayadi pi value. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: distinguish Yukti-dipika from the anonymous Tantrasamgraha-vakhya; manuscript attributions vary, and authorship of the anonymous commentary is unresolved. Do NOT merge Sankara Variyar with the later Sankara Varman of Sadratnamala.

episodes.title: The Illam That Remembered Everything
episodes.region: Vatasseri, Kelallur, Parangngottu and related houses of the Nila valley
episodes.logline: Without a university building, Kerala's illams, teachers, palm leaves and memorized number-verses keep a scientific tradition alive for centuries.
episodes.moral: Institutions can be made from relationships as much as walls.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972)
sources.note: Standard reconstruction of the teacher-pupil chain from Govinda to Acyuta Pisharati.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, Science Texts in Sanskrit in Manuscripts Repositories of Kerala and Tamil Nadu (2003)
sources.note: Survey of manuscript holdings and repositories.

sources.citation: Romila Thapar, Early India (2002), pp. 442-445; Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Context for Brahmin settlements, land grants and mathematical manuscript culture.

episodes.notes: This social innovation story should show how knowledge was organized before modern universities. Sarma reconstructs a chain from Govinda Bhattathiri through Paramesvara, Damodara, Nilakantha, Jyeshthadeva, Sankara Variyar, Acyuta Pisharati and Melpathur. Palm leaves decayed and had to be recopied; Katapayadi verse and oral teaching helped numerical data survive. ACCURACY FLAG: the claim that inheritance customs directly caused mathematical creativity is an argued social explanation, not a primary-source statement. Do NOT invent charters, laboratories or royal academies; the institution was household, temple, teacher and manuscript together.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: Spice Ports and Eclipse Tables
episodes.figure: Kerala Almanac Makers and Port Kerala
episodes.era: Malabar trade and practical astronomy, c. 1340-1620
episodes.region: Calicut, Ponnani, Cochin, temples and ports of the Malabar Coast
episodes.logline: Pepper ships crowd the coast while almanac makers time eclipses, festivals and seasons, showing what accurate astronomy was worth.
episodes.moral: Knowledge flourishes when society has reasons to use it.

sources.citation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, c. 1354; Duarte Barbosa, Book of Duarte Barbosa, c. 1516
sources.note: Primary travel accounts of Calicut and the Malabar spice economy.

sources.citation: Paramesvara, Drigganita, 1431 CE
sources.note: Primary evidence for observation-based correction of astronomical computation.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 217-220; George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011)
sources.note: Modern discussion of practical astronomy and maritime context.

episodes.notes: Use this as an economic context episode, not a false patronage claim. The Malabar coast was tied to Indian Ocean trade; Calicut's Zamorin ruled a pepper-port world known to Ibn Battuta, Barbosa and later Portuguese visitors. Accurate panchangas mattered for ritual timing, agriculture, eclipse observances and civic-temple calendars. ACCURACY FLAGS: there is no document proving the Zamorin commissioned Madhava's series or that navigators needed infinite series. The safe claim is contextual: prosperity, temples, calendars and port society gave astronomical learning social value, while the direct mathematical work remained inside Kerala's scholar networks.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: Acyuta and Melpathur at the Last Flowering
episodes.figure: Acyuta Pisharati and Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri
episodes.era: Late Kerala school and literary synthesis, c. 1550-1621 and after
episodes.region: Trikkandiyur, Guruvayur and Cochin patronage networks, Kerala
episodes.logline: Acyuta Pisharati carries the astronomical chain forward while his student Melpathur reveals how mathematics, grammar and devotion shared one learned world.
episodes.moral: A tradition survives by becoming more than one subject.

sources.citation: Acyuta Pisharati, Uparagakriyakrama, 1592 CE; Malayalam commentary on Madhava's Venvaroha
sources.note: Dated works linking Jyeshthadeva, Acyuta and the continuing Madhava tradition.

sources.citation: Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri, Narayaneeyam and Virakeralaprasasti
sources.note: Literary works showing devotional scholarship and Cochin patronage context.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School (1972), pp. 53-62; P.P. Divakaran, The Mathematics of India (2018)
sources.note: Modern treatment of the late school and Acyuta's technical role.

episodes.notes: Acyuta Pisharati, active around 1550-1621, was from the Pisharadi temple-service community and was a student of Jyeshthadeva; his 1592 Uparagakriyakrama helps anchor the chronology. Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri, his student, is better known for Sanskrit grammar and the devotional Narayaneeyam, but he belongs to the same intellectual ecology. ACCURACY FLAGS: the famous disease-transfer story between Acyuta and Melpathur is hagiographic, not verifiable history; do NOT confuse Melpathur with Narayana Pandita of North India, who was not a Kerala school member.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. The House and the Court

episodes.title: Whish Reads the Palm Leaves
episodes.region: South Malabar, Madras, Cuddapah and the Royal Asiatic Society, London
episodes.logline: A young East India Company official reads palm leaves from Malabar and tells Europe that Indian texts contained infinite series it had not expected to find.
episodes.moral: A forgotten manuscript can reopen the history of ideas.

sources.citation: C.M. Whish, On the Hindu Quadrature of the Circle, Transactions of the Royal Asiatic Society 3:3 (1834), pp. 509-523
sources.note: Primary rediscovery paper on Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasa, Karanapaddhati and Sadratnamala.

sources.citation: John Warren, Kala Sankalita (Madras, 1825)
sources.note: Earlier Western notice of Kerala series in a calendrical study.

sources.citation: Sankara Varman, Sadratnamala, 1819 CE
sources.note: Late traditional Kerala text used by Whish to show the school was still active.

episodes.notes: John Warren noticed the series in 1825, but Whish's 1834 Royal Asiatic Society paper made the famous claim that Kerala shastras contained infinite series and fluxion-like forms. He died in 1833 before the paper appeared; his brother deposited 195 manuscripts at the Royal Asiatic Society in 1836. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: cite the paper as 1834/1835 if needed because the volume dating is confusing. Do NOT say Whish alone discovered the school, and do NOT imply his claim was immediately accepted; it was mostly ignored for about a century.

episodes.title: K V Sarma Unlocks the School
episodes.figure: K V Sarma and C T Rajagopal
episodes.region: Thiruvananthapuram, Madras, Hoshiarpur, Chennai and global scholarship
episodes.logline: After a century of neglect, Indian scholars edit manuscripts, translate proofs and give the Kerala school back to the history of mathematics.
episodes.moral: Recovery takes scholarship as dedicated as discovery.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma, A History of the Kerala School of Hindu Astronomy (1972)
sources.note: Foundational modern monograph establishing authors, lineage and texts.
