sources.citation: C.T. Rajagopal and M.S. Rangachari, Archive for History of Exact Sciences 18 (1978), pp. 89-102
sources.note: Key mathematical recovery and translation of Kerala series material.

sources.citation: K.V. Sarma et al., Ganita-Yukti-Bhasa, 2 vols. (Springer, 2008); Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
sources.note: Complete English Yuktibhasa translation and authoritative modern synthesis.

episodes.notes: C.T. Rajagopal and colleagues translated the series into modern mathematical notation from the 1940s through the 1970s. K.V. Sarma began manuscript work in 1944, edited Venvaroha, Goladipika, Nilakantha's Aryabhatiya-bhasya, Jyotirmimamsa and many more texts, then produced the 1972 history that all later work relies on. His Yuktibhasa translation appeared posthumously in 2008 through Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram. RECENT FLAG: Plofker 2009 and Divakaran 2018 sharpened the source criticism; do NOT treat online summaries as substitutes for manuscript-based scholarship.

episodes.title: The Question Newton Never Answered
episodes.region: Kerala, Portuguese India, European mathematics and modern historiography
episodes.logline: Kerala's series predate Gregory, Newton and Leibniz, but the missing bridge to Europe keeps historians arguing over possibility and proof.
episodes.moral: Priority matters, but evidence matters more.

sources.citation: George Gheverghese Joseph, The Crest of the Peacock, 3rd ed. (2011); D.F. Almeida, J.K. John and A. Zubair, Journal of Natural Geometry 20 (2001)
sources.note: Sources presenting the possibility of Kerala-to-Europe transmission.

sources.citation: David Bressoud, Was Calculus Invented in India?, College Mathematics Journal 33:1 (2002); Victor J. Katz, Mathematics Magazine 68:3 (1995)
sources.note: Careful skeptical assessments of the calculus and transmission claims.

sources.citation: Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009), pp. 251-253
sources.note: Balanced modern statement: possible routes, but no direct manuscript evidence.

episodes.notes: The chronological facts are powerful: Portuguese ships reached Calicut in 1498, Jesuits were active in the 1500s, and Kerala's series predate Gregory, Newton and Leibniz by centuries. But no letter, translation, European citation or manuscript has yet shown that Newton, Leibniz or Gregory knew Kerala mathematics. ACCURACY FLAGS: present transmission as a debated hypothesis, not a proven theft or a settled fact; also do NOT erase Kerala priority for specific series. The strongest honest ending is that Kerala mathematicians achieved remarkable pre-calculus series independently within Indian astronomy, while the European calculus arose as a different, documented synthesis.

episodes.title: The Queen at the Coin Pass
episodes.region: Naneghat pass, Western Ghats, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: At a toll pass between seaports and the Deccan, a Satavahana queen records sacrifices, genealogy, and some of the earliest digit shapes behind modern numerals.
episodes.moral: Names carved with care can outlive armies.

sources.citation: Georg Buhler, 'The Naneghat Inscription,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 4 (1883)
sources.note: Primary publication of the Naneghat cave inscription and royal portrait record.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (Oxford University Press, 1998)
sources.note: Guide to Brahmi, Prakrit inscriptions and palaeographic caution.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent synthesis of Satavahana Prakrit, chronology and epigraphic culture.

episodes.notes: Naneghat linked coastal ports such as Sopara and Kalyan to inland centers such as Nasik, Ter and Pratishthana. Queen Nayanika, also read Naganika by some scholars, probably ruled as regent after Satakarni I and recorded Vedic sacrifices, gifts, genealogy and damaged royal portraits in Maharashtri Prakrit Brahmi. Recent work stresses careful palaeography and new documentation, while Kanaganahalli finds have sharpened early Satavahana chronology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim the inscription contains zero or a full place-value system; it preserves early digit shapes for some numbers. Do NOT call it Buddhist or give a fixed date beyond the c. 2nd-1st century BCE range.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age
episodes.chapter_part: I. Roads Through the Red Earth

episodes.title: The Potsherds Speak at Keezhadi
episodes.era: Vaigai valley urbanism, c. 3rd century BCE-3rd century CE; earlier dates contested
episodes.region: Keezhadi near the Vaigai River, Sivaganga district, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: Under the fields near Madurai, brick structures, dice, ornaments and Tamil Brahmi potsherds reveal a literate urban world while a fierce dating debate continues.
episodes.moral: Good history welcomes discovery without outrunning proof.

sources.citation: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, Keezhadi Excavation Reports, Seasons 4-8
sources.note: Official reports for finds, trenches, AMS samples and site interpretation.

sources.citation: Iravatham Mahadevan, Early Tamil Epigraphy (Harvard Oriental Series, 2003)
sources.note: Standard reference for Tamil Brahmi scripts and dating.

sources.citation: T.S. Subramanian, reports on Keezhadi excavations in The Hindu, 2019-2025
sources.note: Detailed public reporting on excavation phases and the ASI/TNAD dispute.

episodes.notes: Keezhadi was located by ASI archaeologist K. Amarnath Ramakrishna after a Vaigai survey and excavated from 2014 onward, with later phases by the Tamil Nadu archaeology department. Finds include brick structures, graffiti, Tamil Brahmi sherds, terracotta figures, dice, iron objects, punch-marked coins and ornaments; a museum opened in 2023. RECENT FINDINGS: AMS samples have been cited for early dates, but the crucial question is whether inscribed sherds belong to the same secure layer. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the 6th century BCE literacy claim is proven, do NOT identify the site as ancient Madurai, and do NOT treat an unpublished or disputed report as consensus.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age
episodes.chapter_part: I. Roads Through the Red Earth

episodes.title: The Coin That Crushed the Sakas
episodes.era: Satavahana restoration, c. 60-130 CE depending on chronology
episodes.region: Western Deccan, Nasik, Malwa, Saurashtra and Pratishthana
episodes.logline: A king praised by his mother as restorer of Satavahana glory defeats the Saka satraps and stamps his own authority over Nahapana's silver coins.
episodes.moral: Victory is strongest when evidence bears its mark.

sources.citation: R.G. Bhandarkar, 'Inscriptions at Nasik,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1906)
sources.note: Nashik Cave 3 prashasti of Gautami Balashri and related records.

sources.citation: E.J. Rapson, Catalogue of Indian Coins in the British Museum: Andhras, etc. (1908)
sources.note: Classic treatment of Satavahana and Nahapana coinage and overstrikes.

sources.citation: Shailendra Bhandare, 'Numismatic Evidence and Satavahana Chronology,' South Asian Studies (2006)
sources.note: Recent revised chronology based on coins and hoards.

episodes.notes: Gautamiputra is known above all from the Nashik prashasti commissioned by his mother Gautami Balashri in his son Pulumavi's reign. It says he destroyed the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, uprooted the Khakharata line of Nahapana, and restored Satavahana glory. The Jogalthambi hoard of thousands of Nahapana coins overstruck with Gautamiputra's name gives rare material proof of political reversal. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Bhandare, Shimada and Ollett have narrowed but not settled the date debate. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT treat courtly eulogy as literal conquest of every enemy, do NOT say eka-bamhana has one agreed meaning, and do NOT claim the hoard fixes an absolute reign date.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The King Who Gathered Seven Hundred Songs
episodes.figure: King Hala and the Sattasai Poets
episodes.era: Hala tradition c. 1st century CE; anthology redaction c. 2nd-4th century CE
episodes.region: Pratishthana and the Maharashtri Prakrit literary world
episodes.logline: A Satavahana king is remembered for gathering seven hundred Prakrit love poems whose women speak frankly of longing, desire and village life.
episodes.moral: A court becomes great when it listens to many voices.

sources.citation: Peter Khoroche and Herman Tieken, Poems on Life and Love in Ancient India: Hala's Sattasai (SUNY, 2009)
sources.note: Modern English translation and introduction to the anthology.

sources.citation: Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Recent study of Prakrit literary culture and Satavahana language politics.

sources.citation: Sheldon Pollock, The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (University of California Press, 2006)
sources.note: Context for vernacular and cosmopolitan literary economies.

episodes.notes: The Gaha Sattasai, or Gatha Saptashati, is a Maharashtri Prakrit anthology traditionally attributed to King Hala. It preserves hundreds of short lyric poems, many in women's voices, and helped make Maharashtri Prakrit a prestige medium for love poetry. Manuscript traditions name many poets, and Bana cites the work by the 7th century. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Khoroche, Tieken and Ollett emphasize compilation, redaction and the broader language order. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Hala personally wrote all 700 poems, do NOT date the received text securely to the 1st century CE, and do NOT turn early Radha-Krishna references into proof of later theology.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Realm of the Three Crowns
episodes.figure: The Chera, Chola and Pandya Houses
episodes.region: Tamilakam, including Karur, Urayur, Kaveripattinam and Madurai
episodes.logline: Three rival Tamil royal houses appear in Ashoka's edicts and Sangam poems as a world of poets, cattle raids, ports, hill chiefs and shifting honor.
episodes.moral: A shared culture need not mean a single kingdom.

sources.citation: E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum Vol. I, 1925)
sources.note: Ashokan references to Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization Vol. I (1965)
sources.note: Hathigumpha inscription and early external references to Tamil polities.

sources.citation: George L. Hart and Hank Heifetz, Four Hundred Songs of War and Wisdom (Columbia University Press, 1999)
sources.note: Translation of Purananuru poems on kings, chiefs and war.

episodes.notes: Ashoka's edicts mention southern Choda, Pandya, Keralaputra and Satiyaputra realms outside direct Mauryan rule, while Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription may refer to a Tamil confederacy. Sangam poetry names Chera, Chola, Pandya and Velir chiefs, with symbols such as bow, tiger and fish and events like Karikala's Battle of Venni. RECENT WORK by Champakalakshmi and Mahadevan reads these poems alongside archaeology and Tamil Brahmi inscriptions. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present the three crowns as unified Tamil states, do NOT make Ashoka's mention proof of subordination, and do NOT repeat the Grand Anicut engineering story already used in the Chola chapter.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Last Standard Bearer
episodes.era: Late Satavahana power, c. 152-203 CE depending on chronology
episodes.region: Kanheri, Nasik, Nagarjunakonda and the Deccan coasts
episodes.logline: The last great Satavahana ruler reclaims western ground, leaves cave inscriptions far apart, and watches a dynasty's unity fray into successor states.
episodes.moral: A final rally can shine even as an old order fades.

sources.citation: James Burgess, Report on the Buddhist Cave Temples and Their Inscriptions (ASI, 1882)
sources.note: Kanheri inscriptions and western Deccan cave records.

sources.citation: E. Senart, 'Inscriptions at Nasik,' Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8 (1905)
sources.note: Nasik Cave 20 and related late Satavahana records.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Recent chronology linking late Satavahanas, Amaravati and regional transitions.

episodes.notes: Yajna Sri Satakarni is treated by historians as the last major Satavahana king. Kanheri and Nasik inscriptions show his reach, while the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman supplies context for earlier Satavahana-Satrap conflict, though its defeated Satakarni is not Yajna Sri. Ship types on related Satavahana coinage and find-spots point to maritime awareness, but the polity fragmented after him into Abhira, Ikshvaku, Chutu and other successor powers. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT give one exact date, do NOT say one battle ended the dynasty, and do NOT attribute Rudradaman's defeated Satakarni to Yajna Sri.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Jewel on the Krishna
episodes.era: Amaravati great stupa phases, c. 300 BCE-250 CE
episodes.region: Dharanikota-Amaravati on the Krishna River, Andhra Pradesh
episodes.logline: On the Krishna River, queens, merchants, monks and sculptors rebuild a great Buddhist sanctuary whose limestone reliefs travel from Andhra to the world.
episodes.moral: Great art is often the work of generations, not one hand.

sources.citation: James Burgess, The Buddhist Stupas of Amaravati and Jaggayyapeta (1887)
sources.note: Foundational documentation of the monument and inscriptions.

sources.citation: Robert Knox, Amaravati: Buddhist Sculpture from the Great Stupa (British Museum Press, 1992)
sources.note: Catalogue of major surviving sculptures.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context: The Great Stupa at Amaravati (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Modern stratigraphic and art-historical phasing.

episodes.notes: The monument known in inscriptions as the mahacetiya at ancient Dharanikota developed across centuries, with Satavahana-era patronage only one phase. Limestone reliefs in the Amaravati school influenced Buddhist art across Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia and now survive in Chennai, Amaravati and the British Museum after 19th-century removals. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP: Shimada's 2012 study is the key modern phasing, and Kanaganahalli offers important comparison. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ashoka founded Amaravati decisively, do NOT call it a single Satavahana royal project, and do NOT turn the modern repatriation debate into a settled historical claim.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Most Excellent in Jambudvipa
episodes.era: Karla Great Chaitya, c. 50-70 CE with later Satrap and Satavahana gifts
episodes.region: Karla Caves near Lonavala, Maharashtra
episodes.logline: Merchants, monks, guilds and Yavana donors carve a vast rock-cut prayer hall whose banker patron boasts it is the finest in Jambudvipa.
episodes.moral: Shared faith and trade can cut beauty from stone.

sources.citation: H. Luders, A List of Brahmi Inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 10 Appendix (1912)
sources.note: Catalogue of Karla donor inscriptions, including Yavana and merchant gifts.

sources.citation: Vidya Dehejia, Early Buddhist Rock Temples (Thames and Hudson, 1972)
sources.note: Chronological study of early western Deccan rock-cut architecture.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (Brill, 2012)
sources.note: Recent comparison of Buddhist architecture and patronage networks.

episodes.notes: Karla Cave 8 is among South Asia's largest early rock-cut chaitya halls, preserving wooden roof elements and a forest of inscribed pillars. Bhutapala, a setthi from Vaijayanti, declared the rock mansion 'most excellent in Jambudvipa'; several pillars were donated by self-described Yavanas from Denukakata. Later inscriptions by Ushavadata of the Western Satraps and Vasisthiputra Pulumavi show cross-political patronage. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ushavadata built the hall, do NOT assume Yavana means Alexandrian Greek by this date, and do NOT treat Bhutapala's boast as neutral measurement.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Sword That Crossed the World
episodes.era: Sangam-era industry, c. 3rd century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Kodumanal on the Noyyal River, Erode district, Tamil Nadu
episodes.logline: At a trade-route industrial town, Tamil smiths and bead makers help create the high-carbon steel tradition later prized from India to the Islamic world.
episodes.moral: Innovation can begin in furnaces far from royal courts.

sources.citation: K. Rajan, Kodumanal Excavation Report (Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology, 2015)
sources.note: Excavation evidence for industrial production, beads, pottery and inscriptions.

sources.citation: S. Srinivasan, 'Wootz Crucible Steel,' Papers of the Institute of Archaeology Vol. 5 (1994)
sources.note: Foundational modern archaeometallurgical study of south Indian crucible steel.

sources.citation: S. Srinivasan and S. Ranganathan, India's Legendary Wootz Steel (NIAS/IISc, 2004)
sources.note: Technical history of crucible steel production and global reputation.

episodes.notes: Kodumanal, known in Sangam tradition as Kodumanam, stood on an inland route between Malabar and Coromandel trade worlds. Excavations report furnaces, crucibles, Tamil Brahmi sherds, beads of carnelian and other stones, Roman coins and industrial debris. South Indian crucible steel, later called wootz from words such as urukku and ukku, became famous as raw material for blades forged elsewhere. RECENT FINDINGS include scientific analyses of steel residues and Sri Lankan parallels. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say wootz was invented only at Kodumanal, do NOT equate wootz with finished Damascus blades, and do NOT overdate the site beyond its stratigraphic evidence.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Ships Arrive Laden with Gold
episodes.era: Indo-Roman sea trade, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Muzuris on the Malabar coast, Arikamedu, Red Sea ports and Tamilakam
episodes.logline: A Greek trade handbook, Tamil poems, Roman complaints and a Vienna papyrus together reveal pepper ships sailing between India and the Red Sea.
episodes.moral: Commerce can connect worlds while leaving puzzles in its wake.

sources.citation: Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton University Press, 1989)
sources.note: Standard edition and commentary on the Greek trade manual.

sources.citation: Vimala Begley and Richard De Puma, Rome and India: The Ancient Sea Trade (University of Wisconsin Press, 1991)
sources.note: Arikamedu, Roman goods and Indo-Roman exchange.

sources.citation: Matthew A. Cobb, Rome and the Indian Ocean Trade from Augustus to the Early Third Century CE (Brill, 2018)
sources.note: Recent comprehensive study of the network and its documents.

episodes.notes: The Periplus describes Muzuris as a port of large ships and gold, while Akananuru poetry evokes Yavana vessels bringing gold and taking pepper. Pliny complains that India drained Roman wealth, and the Muzuris Papyrus records a cargo loan connected to a voyage of the Hermapollon. Arikamedu yielded amphorae, Arretine ware and beads, while Pattanam excavations have renewed the Muzuris location debate. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT identify Muzuris definitively as Kodungallur or Pattanam, do NOT call Arikamedu a Roman colony, and do NOT treat Pliny's huge sesterces figure as a precise statistic.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Name Carved Beside the Pillar
episodes.era: Deccan donative economy, c. 1st century BCE-3rd century CE
episodes.region: Nasik, Karla, Kanheri, Sanchi and Amaravati
episodes.logline: Across caves and stupas, merchants, monks, nuns and guilds carve their gifts into stone, turning trade wealth into enduring religious institutions.
episodes.moral: Public generosity builds institutions stronger than monuments alone.

sources.citation: H. Luders, A List of Brahmi Inscriptions, Epigraphia Indica Vol. 10 Appendix (1912)
sources.note: Early Brahmi donor inscriptions from caves, pillars, railings and cells.

sources.citation: Gregory Schopen, Bones, Stones, and Buddhist Monks (University of Hawaii Press, 1997)
sources.note: Influential studies of Buddhist monastic donations and endowments.

sources.citation: Jason Neelis, Early Buddhist Transmission and Trade Networks (Brill, 2011)
sources.note: Recent treatment of trade routes, monasteries and donations.

episodes.notes: Satavahana-era inscriptions document donations of pillars, cells, cisterns, caves and villages by setthis, guilds, monks, nuns, queens and officials. Nashik, Karla and Kanheri records reveal immunities, land grants and institutional support; Satavahana lead, copper and potin coins show a pragmatic monetary economy suited to the Deccan. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP stresses these inscriptions as economic evidence rather than royal propaganda alone. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT equate shreni exactly with a medieval European guild, do NOT say kings directed all cave construction, and do NOT call lead coinage primitive merely because it was not gold or silver.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The 1610 Rules of a Language
episodes.era: Layered Tolkappiyam tradition, c. 2nd century BCE-5th century CE debated
episodes.region: Tamilakam and the Madurai literary tradition
episodes.logline: An unknown Tamil grammarian turns sounds, words, landscapes and emotions into a lasting literary system for love, war and public life.
episodes.moral: A language endures when people understand its patterns.

sources.citation: Tolkappiyam, Tamil critical text ed. K.R. Kovintarajan (Tamil University, 1994)
sources.note: Primary grammatical and poetic text in three books.

sources.citation: Kamil Zvelebil, The Smile of Murugan (Brill, 1973)
sources.note: Classic study of Tamil literature and Tolkappiyam dating.

sources.citation: Iravatham Mahadevan, Early Tamil Epigraphy (Harvard Oriental Series, 2003)
sources.note: Pulli mark and Tamil Brahmi arguments relevant to dating.

episodes.notes: The Tolkappiyam is the oldest extant Tamil grammatical work, with sections on letters, words and meaning, including the akam-puram division and tinai system linking landscapes to emotion, flora, fauna, time and poetic situation. Dating is highly contested: some layers may be early, while Mahadevan's pulli argument places important features no earlier than the 2nd century CE and Zvelebil saw later redaction. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Shulman and Tieken keeps the debate alive. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT date it to a legendary ancient Sangam, do NOT insist one historical Tolkappiyar wrote all of it, and do NOT treat the three Sangam academies as historical.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: The Poet Who Guarded Pari's Daughters
episodes.era: Sangam poetic memory, c. 50-200 CE debated
episodes.region: Parambu Nadu and the courts of Tamilakam
episodes.logline: Kapilar sings for the generous Vel Pari, challenges the three crowned kings with poetry, and in later memory protects Pari's orphaned daughters.
episodes.moral: Loyal words can defend the vulnerable when armies fail.

sources.citation: George L. Hart and Hank Heifetz, Four Hundred Songs of War and Wisdom (Columbia University Press, 1999)
sources.note: Purananuru translations including poems linked to Kapilar, Pari and the three crowns.

sources.citation: George L. Hart, The Poems of Ancient Tamil (University of California Press, 1975)
sources.note: Standard introduction to the milieu of Sangam poetry.

sources.citation: David Shulman, Tamil: A Biography (Harvard University Press, 2016)
sources.note: Recent literary history of Tamil and its poets.

episodes.notes: Kapilar is credited by manuscript colophons with over 200 Sangam poems, including mountain-landscape mastery and poems for Vel Pari of Parambu. Purananuru traditions present Pari as a Velir chieftain famous for generosity and besieged by the three crowned kings; later stories say Kapilar sought marriages for Pari's daughters and died by vadakirrutal. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP treats the poems as precious but mediated evidence. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say every attributed poem is certainly by one historical Kapilar, do NOT give precise dates, do NOT call Pari a crowned king, and do NOT present Kapilar's ritual death as directly attested in Sangam poems.
episodes.chapter: The Satavahanas and the Sangam Age

episodes.title: Tarabai Outlasts Aurangzeb
episodes.region: Satara, Kolhapur, the Deccan, Malwa and Gujarat
episodes.logline: After Rajaram dies, Tarabai holds a mobile kingdom together and keeps Maratha resistance alive until Aurangzeb's exhausted armies fade.
episodes.moral: Leadership can survive when courage serves a larger duty.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhabu-l-Lubab, sections on the late Deccan war
sources.note: Hostile Mughal-side testimony for Maratha resistance after Rajaram's death.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. II, chapters on Tarabai and Shahu
sources.note: Synthesis drawing on bakhars and Marathi administrative materials.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern account of the succession crisis, Tarabai's regency and state formation.

episodes.notes: Tarabai, daughter of Hambirrao Mohite and widow of Rajaram I, acted as regent for her son Shivaji II from 1700 as Mughal armies pressed Satara and the Deccan. KEY FACTS: Maratha raids reached Malwa and Gujarat before Aurangzeb died at Ahmadnagar in 1707; Shahu's release then split Maratha politics, and Tarabai's Kolhapur court survived after the Battle of Khed in 1708. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Gordon, Guha and Deshpande treat her as a strategic political actor later marginalized by Peshwa-centered memory. Do NOT claim she personally led every raid from horseback; some battle details come from retrospective bakhars and must be treated cautiously.

episodes.title: Balaji Vishwanath Writes a New State
episodes.era: Rise of the hereditary Peshwa, 1713-1720 CE
episodes.region: Satara, Pune and Mughal Delhi
episodes.logline: A Konkan accountant becomes Peshwa and turns Maratha power into a recognized fiscal and constitutional system.
episodes.moral: Institutions can outlast the victories that create them.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Balaji Vishwanath letters and early Shahu-period documents
sources.note: Primary Modi-script administrative evidence for the early Peshwa system.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhabu-l-Lubab, account of the Syed Brothers and Delhi politics
sources.note: Persian narrative context for the 1719 Mughal settlement.

sources.citation: Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India (Cambridge UP, 1986)
sources.note: Key interpretation of chauth, sardeshmukhi and Maratha sovereignty claims.

episodes.notes: Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa in 1713 and in 1719 helped the Syed Brothers at Delhi while securing Mughal recognition of Maratha chauth and sardeshmukhi rights in the six Deccan provinces, plus the release of Shahu's mother Yesubai. KEY FACTS: his office became hereditary when Bajirao succeeded in 1720, shifting real power from Satara toward Pune. RECENT FINDINGS: modern state-formation work reads this as a fiscal-military constitution rather than a simple heroic rise. Do NOT present colorful bakhar stories about secret persuasion or Shahu's recognition as unverified fact.

episodes.title: Palkhed Without a Pitched Battle
episodes.region: Pune, Berar, Khandesh, Gujarat, Palkhed and Mungi-Shevgaon
episodes.logline: Bajirao refuses the Nizam's heavy army a grand battle and wins by speed, water, supplies and strategic patience.
episodes.moral: The smartest victory may be won before swords cross.

sources.citation: Selections from the Peshwa Daftar, ed. G.S. Sardesai, letters for the 1727-1728 campaign
sources.note: Administrative correspondence for movements and negotiations.

sources.citation: Treaty of Mungi-Shevgaon, 6 March 1728
sources.note: Documented settlement recognizing Maratha claims after the Palkhed campaign.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, Marathas, Marauders, and State Formation (OUP, 1994)
sources.note: Modern reading of campaigns as revenue and sovereignty operations, not pure conquest.

episodes.notes: In 1727-1728 Bajirao answered Nizam-ul-Mulk's challenge by avoiding a set-piece battle, striking Berar, Mahur and Washim, threatening Burhanpur, and trapping the Nizam near Palkhed before the 6 March 1728 treaty. KEY ACCURACY FLAGS: this is not the already existing 1737 Delhi ride; it is a distinct logistics story about mobile cavalry and a heavier artillery army. Recent scholarship warns against turning Bajirao into an always-undefeated legend; do NOT ignore earlier setbacks or the Nizam's own logistical mistakes.

episodes.title: Kanhoji Angre Rules the Western Seas
episodes.region: Suvarnadurg, Khanderi, Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg, Bombay and the Konkan coast
episodes.logline: From sea forts and swift vessels, Kanhoji Angre makes European companies bargain with a Maratha admiral they called a pirate.
episodes.moral: Control of the coast can protect freedom inland.

sources.citation: British East India Company records on failed operations against Angre, 1718-1722
sources.note: European primary evidence for repeated unsuccessful attacks.

sources.citation: Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, Portuguese records on Angre and the Konkan
sources.note: Portuguese imperial documentation for western-coast conflict and commerce.

sources.citation: Rene Barendse, Arabian Seas 1700-1763, Vol. I (Brill, 2009)
sources.note: Recent archive-based reassessment of Angre's origins and maritime politics.

episodes.notes: Kanhoji Angre commanded Maratha coastal power from about 1698 and, after a 1713 settlement with Balaji Vishwanath, was recognized as Sarkhel with forts and coastal posts. KEY FACTS: British-Portuguese efforts in 1718, 1720, 1721 and 1722 failed, and his sea forts later formed part of the 2025 Maratha Military Landscapes evidence base. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP FLAG: Barendse complicates nationalist and European labels alike; do NOT state a certain caste or ethnic origin, and do NOT accept the European word 'pirate' without explaining the contested admiral/privateer framing.

episodes.title: Chimaji Appa Opens Vasai's Gates
episodes.region: Thane, Salsette, Arnala, Tarapur and Vasai on the Konkan coast
episodes.logline: Chimaji Appa takes fort after fort until Portuguese Bassein stands isolated and the northern Konkan changes hands.
episodes.moral: Patient preparation can break the strongest wall.

sources.citation: Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, Portuguese records of the Vasai campaign
sources.note: Primary Portuguese accounts for the siege and loss of Bassein.

sources.citation: Chimaji Appa's Modi-script letter to Nanasaheb Peshwa on the campaign
sources.note: Maratha-side primary correspondence preserved in Deccan archives.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern context for the campaign's revenue and coastal consequences.

episodes.notes: The Vasai campaign was a methodical reduction of Portuguese positions: Arnala in 1737, Thane and Salsette, Dahanu and Mahim, then Vasai on 16 May 1739. KEY FACTS: the victory ended Portuguese dominance north of Goa and transferred forts, trade routes and military infrastructure to Maratha control. Recent military scholarship emphasizes logistics and siege adaptation, not just bravery. Do NOT treat later temple-bell or devotional anecdotes as certain, and do NOT use exact casualty totals without source caveats.

episodes.title: Panipat on Makar Sankranti
episodes.region: Delhi, Panipat, Awadh, Rohilkhand and Pune
episodes.logline: A starving Maratha camp breaks out at Panipat, where a day of courage and miscalculation becomes a wound in imperial memory.
episodes.moral: Ambition without supplies and allies can become tragedy.

sources.citation: Kashi Raja's Bakhar, eyewitness account from Shuja-ud-Daula's circle
sources.note: Often treated as the strongest primary narrative for the battle.

sources.citation: James Grant Duff, A History of the Marathas, Vol. II (1826)
sources.note: Early history using survivor testimony, valuable but colonial in perspective.

sources.citation: Uday S. Kulkarni, Solstice at Panipat: 14 January 1761 (2011)
sources.note: Recent synthesis using primary narratives and later scholarship.

episodes.notes: Sadashivrao Bhau's northern army secured Delhi in 1760 but was blockaded by Ahmad Shah Durrani, Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula before the breakout on 14 January 1761. KEY FACTS: Ibrahim Khan Gardi's artillery, Vishwasrao's death, mass casualties and prisoner killings are strongly attested, while precise numbers vary. Recent scholarship treats defeat as multi-causal: logistics, alliance failures, non-combatant burden and Confederacy structure. Do NOT claim Bhau certainly escaped; most scholars accept he died, but body-identification stories remain contested.

episodes.title: Madhavrao Rebuilds the Broken Tent
episodes.region: Pune, Rakshasbhuvan, Mysore, Dharwad and Delhi
episodes.logline: A teenage Peshwa inherits ruin and uses discipline, campaigns and revenue reform to make Maratha power stand again.
episodes.moral: Recovery begins when grief becomes disciplined work.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar records for Madhavrao I's administration and campaigns
sources.note: Primary administrative evidence for reform, orders and revenue discipline.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. III (1948)
sources.note: Detailed narrative of Madhavrao's recovery period.

sources.citation: Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818 (Cambridge UP, 1993)
sources.note: Modern assessment of post-Panipat reconstruction and limits.

episodes.notes: Madhavrao I became Peshwa in June 1761 at age sixteen and, despite conflict with Raghunathrao and tuberculosis, restored authority against the Nizam at Rakshasbhuvan in 1763, pushed Mysore campaigns, and saw Mahadji Scindia restore Shah Alam II to Delhi in 1771. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP highlights fiscal discipline and officer accountability as much as battlefield success. Do NOT imply Punjab was recovered after Panipat, and do NOT turn every later praise of Madhavrao into contemporary evidence.

episodes.title: Forts Where the Mountains Fought
episodes.era: Maratha military landscapes, 1645-1818 CE; UNESCO inscription 2025
episodes.region: Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg and the Sahyadris
episodes.logline: Cisterns, hidden gates, sea walls and mountain paths turn Maratha forts into an engineered network of survival.
episodes.moral: Good design can make courage endure.

sources.citation: Henry Oxienden's 1674 English report from Raigad
sources.note: Eyewitness description of Raigad during Shivaji's coronation context.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Maratha Military Landscapes of India nomination and 2025 listing materials
sources.note: Recent archaeological and conservation survey of the fort network.

sources.citation: M.S. Naravane, Forts of Maharashtra (1995); Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818
sources.note: Architectural and historical interpretations of the fort system.

episodes.notes: Maratha fort engineering combined hill forts, sea forts, cisterns, granaries, bent entrances, sally ports and coastal bases so a weaker field army could survive stronger imperial forces. KEY FACTS: Raigad, Sindhudurg, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg, Khanderi and other forts were surveyed in the Maratha Military Landscapes nomination and listed by UNESCO in 2025 after debate. RECENT FINDINGS: ICOMOS questioned whether the forts were proven as one integrated system, so present the network as a historical and conservation argument, not a settled engineering blueprint. Do NOT present Hirakani or handprint traditions as independently verified.

episodes.title: Tukaram's Songs Walk to Pandharpur
episodes.figure: Sant Tukaram and the Warkari poets
episodes.era: Warkari memory and Maratha society, c. 1608-present
episodes.region: Dehu, Alandi, Paithan and Pandharpur
episodes.logline: Vernacular songs and the Pandharpur Wari give ordinary people a shared moral language beyond court and battlefield.
episodes.moral: A people's songs can carry equality farther than orders can.

sources.citation: Tukaram Gatha, manuscript tradition and 1869 printed edition
sources.note: Core abhangas attributed to Tukaram, with textual layers requiring caution.

sources.citation: Mahipati, Bhaktavijay and Bhaktalilamrut, 18th century
sources.note: Hagiographic source preserving Warkari memory and saint traditions.

sources.citation: Christian Lee Novetzke, Religion and Public Memory (Columbia UP, 2008)
sources.note: Modern study of bhakti memory, performance and public tradition.

episodes.notes: The Warkari tradition linked Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath, Tukaram and later pilgrimage practice around Vitthal of Pandharpur. KEY FACTS: Tukaram's abhangas circulated in manuscripts before the 1869 printed Gatha; Narayan Maharaj is associated with formalizing the paduka procession in 1685. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP reads saint memory as public practice, not simple biography. Do NOT claim Shivaji certainly met Tukaram, do NOT state Ramdas was certainly Shivaji's guru, and do NOT narrate Tukaram's bodily ascent to Vaikuntha as history.

episodes.title: Gold Thread in Paithan and Yeola
episodes.era: Textile economies under Maratha patronage, 17th-18th centuries CE
episodes.region: Paithan, Yeola, Maheshwar, Surat and Mandu
episodes.logline: Silk, zari, reversible borders and relocated looms show how craft communities turned patronage into economic innovation.
episodes.moral: Skilled hands can weave economies as well as cloth.

sources.citation: Ptolemy, Geographia Book VII, reference to Baithana
sources.note: Early external notice linking Paithan with long-distance textile geography.

sources.citation: Nevasa excavation reports, 1966, silk fragments near Paithan
sources.note: Material evidence for early Deccan textile traditions.

sources.citation: Geographical Indications Registry of India, Paithani and Maheshwari Sari and Fabrics GI documents, 2010
sources.note: Recent official documentation of craft history, technique and communities.

episodes.notes: Paithani weaving had ancient roots at Paithan and was reshaped under later Deccan and Maratha patronage as Yeola became a major weaving center; Maheshwari weaving grew at Maheshwar with traditions of invited artisans from Surat and Mandu. KEY FACTS: distinctive Paithani tapestry techniques, peacock motifs and zari work, and Maheshwari reversible borders show technical craft innovation; GI records in 2010 preserve modern community histories. Do NOT claim an exact Peshwa relocation date without evidence, and do NOT say Ahilyabai personally designed the first Maheshwari sari as proven fact.

episodes.title: The Chauth That Became Sovereignty
episodes.figure: Shahu I and the Maratha revenue officers
episodes.region: Pune, Satara, Malwa, Gujarat, Nagpur, Baroda and Gwalior
episodes.logline: Chauth, sardeshmukhi, hundis and coins turn scattered cavalry claims into a fiscal web across India.
episodes.moral: A state is held together by accounts as much as armies.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar revenue accounts and campaign financial orders
sources.note: Primary Modi-script evidence for collections, assignments and military finance.

sources.citation: Maratha Shivrai and Peshwa-era rupee coinage catalogued by the Numismatic Society of India
sources.note: Material evidence for monetary sovereignty and decentralized mints.

sources.citation: Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India (Cambridge UP, 1986)
sources.note: Classic argument that chauth expressed sovereignty, not merely protection money.

episodes.notes: Maratha finance rested on chauth, sardeshmukhi, revenue assignments, moneylenders, hundis and multiple mints, including Shivrai coin traditions and later Peshwa, Holkar, Scindia, Bhonsle and Gaekwad issues. KEY FACTS: the 1719 Mughal recognition mattered because it converted pressure into a legal imperial claim; collections were divided among center, officers and troops. RECENT SCHOLARSHIP by Wink, Gordon and Guha debates whether this was extraction, sovereignty, state formation or all three. Do NOT call chauth only 'protection money,' and do NOT invent precise banking-house amounts where Daftar evidence is incomplete.

episodes.title: Mahadji Scindia Drills a New Army
episodes.figure: Mahadji Scindia and Benoit de Boigne
episodes.region: Gwalior, Delhi, Agra, Hindustan and the Chambal region
episodes.logline: Mahadji Scindia hires de Boigne and forges drilled infantry that can guard Delhi with muskets, artillery and regular pay.
episodes.moral: Learning from rivals can become strength when guided by purpose.

sources.citation: James Grant Duff, A History of the Marathas, Vol. III (1826)
sources.note: Early narrative using Maratha and British materials for Scindia's late eighteenth-century power.

sources.citation: Benoit de Boigne memoir traditions and European accounts of Scindia's service
sources.note: Primary-adjacent testimony for the campoo brigades, read with caution.

sources.citation: Randolf Cooper, The Anglo-Maratha Campaigns and the Contest for India (Cambridge UP, 2003)
sources.note: Modern military analysis of European-drilled forces and Anglo-Maratha conflict.

episodes.notes: After restoring Mughal emperor Shah Alam II to Delhi in 1771 and becoming a northern kingmaker, Mahadji Scindia employed Benoit de Boigne from the mid-1780s to organize regular infantry brigades, artillery and disciplined campoo formations. KEY FACTS: this was a major military innovation inside the Confederacy, pairing Maratha finance and politics with European drill before Scindia's death in 1794. Recent scholarship warns that modernization was uneven and dependent on pay, commanders and regional revenue. Do NOT portray de Boigne as single-handedly modernizing all Maratha armies, and do NOT treat Delhi's Mughal emperor as holding independent power by this time.

episodes.title: Nana Fadnavis and the Twelve Pillars
episodes.era: Barabhai Council and late Confederacy diplomacy, 1773-1800 CE
episodes.region: Pune, Salbai, Wadgaon, Delhi and the Deccan courts
episodes.logline: After a palace murder, Nana Fadnavis builds a council, guards an infant Peshwa and keeps rival powers balanced for a generation.
episodes.moral: Patient diplomacy can hold a fragile house together.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Nana Fadnavis letters, roznishi and diplomatic dispatches
sources.note: Large primary archive for late Maratha governance and intelligence.

sources.citation: Treaty of Wadgaon, 1779, and Treaty of Salbai, 1782, in British and Maratha records
sources.note: Documented instruments marking First Anglo-Maratha War outcomes.

sources.citation: Prachi Deshpande, Creative Pasts (Columbia UP, 2007); Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818
sources.note: Modern interpretations of Nana's memory, diplomacy and limitations.

episodes.notes: Nana Fadnavis helped form the Barabhai Council after Narayanrao Peshwa's assassination in 1773, protected Madhavrao II's claim, and managed diplomacy through the First Anglo-Maratha War, Wadgaon in 1779 and Salbai in 1782. KEY FACTS: his papers make this period unusually document-rich; Grant Duff's 'Maratha Machiavelli' label is influential but colonial. Recent scholarship stresses collective politics and Nana's failures as well as skill, including tensions with Tipu, Scindia and the British. Do NOT make him the sole brain of the Confederacy, and do NOT quote the famous Tipu-death remark as certain exact wording.

episodes.title: Guru Nanak and the River That Spoke
episodes.region: Rai Bhoi di Talvandi, Sultanpur Lodhi, Kartarpur and the Punjab
episodes.logline: After vanishing at the Bein River, Nanak returns with a message beyond Hindu and Muslim labels and builds a singing, working community at Kartarpur.
episodes.moral: Truth grows when people share work, song and bread.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak's hymns including the Babur Vani passages
sources.note: Primary evidence for Nanak's teaching and rare historical anchors in the 1520s.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, c. 1600-1636
sources.note: Early Sikh account before many later janamsakhi elaborations.

sources.citation: W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968); S.S. Padam ed., Sakhi Mahal Pehle Ki (2014)
sources.note: Modern source criticism and the recently published early tradition.

episodes.notes: Nanak was born in 1469 at Rai Bhoi di Talvandi, worked at Sultanpur Lodhi under Daulat Khan Lodi, and settled around 1521 at Kartarpur, where the sangat, shared labor and langar became the seed of Sikh community life. Recent source criticism is vital: the Guru Granth Sahib preserves his own hymns, while janamsakhis were written after his death and often expand miracle stories. Sakhi Mahal Pehle Ki, published by S.S. Padam in 2014 and linked to an older tradition, lacks many famous travel episodes, so do NOT claim exact four-udasi routes, Mecca conversations, or the three-day river disappearance as verifiable biography; tell them as Sikh tradition around a securely attested teacher.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Guru Angad Shapes the Living Letters
episodes.era: Second Guru and early Sikh literacy, c. 1539-1552 CE
episodes.region: Khadur Sahib, Tarn Taran district, Punjab
episodes.logline: Lehna becomes Angad and gives the growing community a clear script, schools and songs that ordinary Punjabi children can learn.
episodes.moral: A shared alphabet can turn faith into a living school.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, 62 hymns of Guru Angad
sources.note: Textual and manuscript evidence of early Gurmukhi use.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1
sources.note: Early Sikh source crediting Angad's role in the script tradition.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998); Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001)
sources.note: Modern account of Gurmukhi's structure and early manuscripts.

episodes.notes: Guru Angad, born Lehna in 1504, succeeded Guru Nanak in 1539 and worked from Khadur Sahib, where tradition remembers akharas, free schools, and a disciplined langar. His innovation was not magic invention but standardization: Gurmukhi drew on Landa, Sharda and local scripts, then became a stable 35-letter system suited to Punjabi and to preserving the Gurus' hymns. The Goindval Pothis and other late 16th-century manuscripts are important material evidence. ACCURACY FLAG: do NOT say Angad invented writing or created Gurmukhi in a single moment; say he codified and spread a script that made Sikh scripture and Punjabi literacy durable.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Guru Amar Das Builds the Steps of Equality
episodes.era: Third Guru and social reform, c. 1552-1574 CE
episodes.region: Goindval on the Beas River, Punjab
episodes.logline: At Goindval, the old Guru builds a baoli, seats rich and poor in one langar, and teaches that women may lead and widows need not burn.
episodes.moral: Equality becomes real when it is practiced before every meal.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das's Var Suhi and other hymns
sources.note: Primary text for his anti-sati teaching and devotional program.

sources.citation: Goindval Pothis, late 16th century
sources.note: Pre-canonical Sikh manuscript collections tied to Guru Amar Das's family.

sources.citation: Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001); Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (2011)
sources.note: Recent scholarship on manuscripts, women and reform.

episodes.notes: Guru Amar Das became Guru in 1552, established Goindval, and built the 84-step baoli as both sacred and civic water infrastructure. His hymns condemn sati by redefining the true sati as spiritual fidelity, not a widow's death; tradition also credits him with opposing purdah, appointing women through the piri system, organizing 22 manjis, and strengthening dasvandh, the one-tenth community contribution. Recent scholarship highlights these as social and economic institutions, not only devotional teachings. ACCURACY FLAGS: Akbar's visit and exact conversations at langar are plausible Sikh tradition rather than firm imperial record; do NOT attach modern Anand Karaj circumambulation practices directly to his age.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Guru Ram Das Digs the Pool of Nectar
episodes.region: Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, Punjab
episodes.logline: The fourth Guru turns a dusty settlement into Ramdaspur, calling merchants, artisans and pilgrims around a new pool of nectar.
episodes.moral: A city can be built around service instead of pride.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Ram Das's hymns including the Lavan
sources.note: Primary evidence for his literary contribution.

sources.citation: Gazetteer of the Amritsar District (1892)
sources.note: Colonial record preserving the 700-rupee land-purchase tradition.

sources.citation: Pardeep Singh Arshi, The Golden Temple: History, Art and Architecture (1989); Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed (2013)
sources.note: Architectural and historical context for Amritsar.

episodes.notes: Guru Ram Das, born Jetha in 1534, became Guru in 1574 and developed Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, around excavated sarovars that became the center of Sikh urban life. The story is an innovation in city-making: dasvandh donations, invited craftsmen and traders, water management, pilgrimage and commerce all strengthened one another. He composed 638 hymns, including the Lavan. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: the present sarovar and shrine have been rebuilt many times, though the 16th-century site is secure; the 700-rupee purchase from Tung village comes through later records; do NOT claim the modern Anand Karaj circumambulation rite was fully fixed by Guru Ram Das, because scholars place that ritual formalization in the Singh Sabha period.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Sacred Word and the Pool

episodes.title: Guru Arjan Gathers the Many Voices
episodes.era: Compilation of the Adi Granth and first Sikh martyrdom, c. 1604-1606 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Goindval, Lahore and the Mughal Punjab
episodes.logline: To protect the songs from forgery, Guru Arjan gathers Gurus, bhagats and Sufi voices into the Adi Granth and places it at Harmandir Sahib.
episodes.moral: A true book can make room for many voices.

sources.citation: Adi Granth tradition; GNDU Manuscript 1245, c. 1599, and related early pothis
sources.note: Material evidence for pre-canonical recensions and compilation.

sources.citation: Jahangir, Tuzk-e-Jahangiri, early 17th century
sources.note: Contemporary Mughal account of Guru Arjan's arrest and death.

sources.citation: Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (2001); Pashaura Singh, Life and Work of Guru Arjan (2006)
sources.note: Recent manuscript and biography scholarship.

episodes.notes: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth with Bhai Gurdas as scribe and installed it at Harmandir Sahib on 1 September 1604 with Baba Buddha as first granthi. It is a scholarly and artistic innovation: hymns arranged by ragas, including Sikh Gurus and saint-poets such as Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid across languages and social backgrounds. Jahangir's memoir confirms Arjan's death in Mughal custody in 1606, while Sikh tradition remembers him as the first martyr. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Gurinder Singh Mann shows multiple drafts and pre-canonical manuscripts; the Kartarpur Bir is revered but debated, so do NOT assert its provenance as settled; do NOT state specific torture methods as proven by Jahangir's text.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh
episodes.chapter_part: II. The Sacred Word and the Pool

episodes.title: Guru Hargobind Raises Two Swords
episodes.era: Miri-Piri and early Sikh militarization, c. 1606-1644 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Gwalior Fort, Kartarpur and Kiratpur Sahib
episodes.logline: After his father's death, Hargobind wears two swords for spirit and worldly duty, then raises the Akal Takht across from the shrine.
episodes.moral: Justice needs prayer, courage and responsibility together.

sources.citation: Varan Bhai Gurdas, including Vaar 26
sources.note: Early Sikh testimony for Hargobind's age.

sources.citation: Early Sikh hukamnamas from Guru Hargobind's period
sources.note: Evidence for institutions and the evolving term Khalsa.

sources.citation: Louis E. Fenech and W.H. McLeod, Historical Dictionary of Sikhism (2014); Pashaura Singh's studies on early Sikh history
sources.note: Modern synthesis and dating cautions.

episodes.notes: Guru Hargobind succeeded Guru Arjan in 1606 and symbolized miri-piri by wearing two swords, linking spiritual authority with worldly protection. The Akal Takht at Amritsar made that idea architectural: a temporal throne facing the Harmandir Sahib. His Gwalior imprisonment and later armed conflicts with Mughal forces are broadly attested, and recent hukamnama work shows terms like Khalsa predate the famous 1699 formalization. ACCURACY FLAGS: dates for his birth and Gwalior imprisonment vary; the Bandi Chhor story of 52 freed princes and cloak threads is beloved Sikh tradition but not epigraphically confirmed, so present it as tradition, not a literal court record.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Stands at Delhi
episodes.era: Ninth Guru and religious freedom, c. 1664-1675 CE
episodes.region: Anandpur Sahib, Delhi, Punjab, Bihar, Bengal and Assam
episodes.logline: The quiet ninth Guru faces Aurangzeb's power at Delhi, choosing death rather than letting conscience be crushed.
episodes.moral: Freedom of faith is worth defending even for others.

sources.citation: Bachittar Natak, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, c. late 17th century
sources.note: Primary Sikh framing of Guru Tegh Bahadur's sacrifice.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns and salokas of Guru Tegh Bahadur
sources.note: Direct evidence of his thought and devotional voice.

sources.citation: Louis E. Fenech, Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition (2000); Satish Chandra, Medieval India (2001)
sources.note: Modern analysis of Sikh and Persian source conflicts.

episodes.notes: Guru Tegh Bahadur, born Tyag Mal in 1621, became the ninth Guru in 1664 and travelled widely before his execution at Delhi on 11 November 1675 under Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition calls him Hind ki Chadar, the shield of India, because he died for the right of others to worship freely. The sources problem is central: Sikh accounts emphasize martyrdom and conscience, while later Persian accounts frame him as a political rebel or bandit; both agree that he was executed. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Fenech treats martyrdom narratives as theological as well as historical; the Kashmiri Pandit delegation appears in later tradition and is not in Bachittar Natak, so do NOT present it as independently proven.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Guru Gobind Singh Calls the Five
episodes.figure: Guru Gobind Singh and the Panj Pyare
episodes.region: Anandpur Sahib, Chamkaur, Sirhind and Nanded
episodes.logline: At Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh calls five volunteers from distant regions and shapes the Khalsa into a fearless community of equals.
episodes.moral: Courage becomes stronger when shared by all.

sources.citation: Senapatii, Sri Gur Sobha, c. 1711
sources.note: Near-contemporary account of Guru Gobind Singh's final years.

sources.citation: Hukamnamas of Guru Gobind Singh, c. 1699-1708
sources.note: Primary documents for Khalsa identity and discipline.

sources.citation: W.H. McLeod, Sikhism (1997); Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Birth of the Khalsa (2005)
sources.note: Contrasting critical and sympathetic scholarly readings.

episodes.notes: Guru Gobind Singh, born at Patna in 1666, became Guru after his father's martyrdom and formally shaped the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699. The Panj Pyare came from different regions and social backgrounds, and the rahit with the Five Ks made a visible, disciplined community; later events at Chamkaur, Sirhind and Nanded turned the story into one of sacrifice and succession to the Guru Granth Sahib. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: the earliest near-contemporary Sri Gur Sobha does not contain the full dramatic tent-and-heads scene, which appears in later tradition; say Sikh tradition narrates it, not that every detail is proven. Also note that Khalsa language appears in earlier hukamnamas, so 1699 was formalization, not creation from nothing.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Banda Bahadur Strikes the First Sikh Coin
episodes.era: First Sikh state and land reform, c. 1708-1716 CE
episodes.region: Nanded, Sirhind, Lohgarh and the Punjab hills
episodes.logline: A former hermit rides north, defeats Sirhind, gives land to tillers, and strikes coins in the Gurus' names rather than his own.
episodes.moral: Victory is noblest when it lifts the poor.

sources.citation: Banda Singh Bahadur's Sikh rupees, Amritsar and Mukhlisgarh-Lohgarh mints, c. 1711
sources.note: Physical evidence for Sikh sovereignty and coin legends.

sources.citation: Akhbar-i-Darbar-i-Mualla and Ibratnama, early 18th-century Persian records
sources.note: Contemporary and near-contemporary evidence for campaigns and execution.

sources.citation: Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks (2011); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Recent and standard studies of 18th-century Sikh political formation.

episodes.notes: Madho Das, renamed Banda Singh Bahadur after meeting Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded in 1708, led a fast northern campaign and captured Sirhind on 22 May 1710. His government at Lohgarh is remembered for abolishing zamindari in controlled areas and granting land rights to cultivators, a major economic and social innovation. His coins named Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, not Banda, establishing a Sikh numismatic principle later continued by the Misls and Ranjit Singh. ACCURACY FLAGS: conversion-meeting details and miracles are hagiographic; do NOT claim his caste background from later polemics, because contemporary Mughal records do not support it; his 1716 execution is historical but should be handled without gore.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: The Sarbat Khalsa Votes Without a King
episodes.figure: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and the Dal Khalsa
episodes.era: Misl confederacy and collective sovereignty, c. 1716-1799 CE
episodes.region: Amritsar, Lahore and the wider Punjab
episodes.logline: After persecution scatters the Sikhs into bands, the Sarbat Khalsa gathers at Amritsar to make binding decisions without a king.
episodes.moral: A people can survive when they learn to decide together.

sources.citation: Gobindshahi and Nanakshahi Sikh coins from Lahore and Amritsar mints
sources.note: Physical evidence for Misl-era sovereignty and limits on personal rule.

sources.citation: Ratan Singh Bhangu, Prachin Panth Prakash, c. 1809
sources.note: Key Sikh chronicle of the Misl period.

sources.citation: Purnima Dhavan, When Sparrows Became Hawks (2011); J.S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1998)
sources.note: Recent interpretation of the warrior tradition and confederacy.

episodes.notes: After Banda Singh Bahadur's death, Sikh jathas survived persecution and developed the Sarbat Khalsa, a collective assembly at Amritsar whose gurmatas were binding on the community. In 1748 the forces were organized into Misls under Dal Khalsa leadership, with Jassa Singh Ahluwalia prominent; Misl-era coins make sovereignty visible. This is a political innovation story: collective authority after the human Gurus, with egalitarian ideals under military pressure. ACCURACY FLAGS: casualty numbers for the Chhota and Vadda Ghallughara vary sharply, so avoid exact totals; do NOT call the system a modern democracy without qualification, because it was a confederate, religious-military assembly with uneven regional power.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Ranjit Singh Enters Lahore
episodes.era: Unification of the Sikh Empire, c. 1799-1809 CE
episodes.region: Gujranwala, Lahore, Amritsar and the Sutlej frontier
episodes.logline: A young misl chief enters Lahore, becomes Maharaja, and builds a plural court where coins honor the Gurus instead of himself.
episodes.moral: The strongest rule can still choose humility.

sources.citation: Sohan Lal Suri, Umdat-ut-Tawarikh, c. 1805-1849
sources.note: Court chronicle for dates, campaigns and administration.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840); Baron Charles Hugel, Travels in Kashmir and the Panjab (1845)
sources.note: Eyewitness European descriptions of the Lahore Durbar.

sources.citation: Priya Atwal, Royals and Rebels: The Rise and Fall of the Sikh Empire (2020)
sources.note: Recent archival study of court, family and succession politics.

episodes.notes: Ranjit Singh, born in 1780 at Gujranwala, entered Lahore on 7 July 1799 and was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801. His court was multi-faith and multilingual, with Fakir Azizuddin, Dina Nath, Dogra nobles, Sikh sardars and European officers all serving the state. Multiple European visitors report that he avoided the death penalty, while his Nanakshahi coins carried the Gurus' names rather than his own. The 1809 Treaty of Amritsar fixed the Sutlej boundary with the British and bought Punjab three decades of independence. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: Priya Atwal complicates simple hero tales with court, family and succession politics; do NOT treat every wisdom anecdote as documented fact.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: The Army That Learned from Napoleon
episodes.era: Fauj-i-Khas and military modernization, c. 1822-1839 CE
episodes.region: Lahore, Peshawar, Jamrud and Manikyala
episodes.logline: Ranjit Singh hires veterans of Napoleon to train infantry, artillery and cavalry, while Sikh generals guard the road to the Khyber.
episodes.moral: Learning from others can strengthen your own house.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840)
sources.note: Eyewitness source for the army and European officers.

sources.citation: Jean-Marie Lafont, Maharaja Ranjit Singh: Lord of the Five Rivers (2002); Charles Grey, European Adventurers of Northern India (1929)
sources.note: Studies of Allard, Ventura, Avitabile and Court.

sources.citation: Jean-Baptiste Ventura's Manikyala excavation reports, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1830s
sources.note: Primary scholarly record of an early stupa excavation by a Lahore officer.

episodes.notes: After 1809, Ranjit Singh modernized beyond cavalry. Jean-Francois Allard and Jean-Baptiste Ventura arrived in Lahore in 1822, later joined by Paolo Avitabile and Claude Auguste Court, and helped train the Fauj-i-Khas with European-style infantry, cavalry and artillery. Hari Singh Nalwa's frontier campaigns, including Peshawar and Jamrud, show that the empire combined imported drill with Sikh and Punjabi command. Ventura's 1830 Manikyala stupa excavation adds an unexpected scholarly innovation. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT portray Europeans as the sole creators of Sikh strength; the regular army worked because Ranjit Singh, local commanders, artillery workshops and Punjabi soldiers adapted foreign techniques to their own state.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: Ranjit Singh Clothes the Temple in Gold
episodes.era: Golden Temple restoration and sacred kingship, c. 1802-1839 CE
episodes.region: Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
episodes.logline: After decades of rebuilding, Ranjit Singh covers Harmandir Sahib in gold and turns royal wealth into a shining offering for all pilgrims.
episodes.moral: The finest treasure is the one shared with everyone.

sources.citation: Sohan Lal Suri, Umdat-ut-Tawarikh, c. 1805-1849
sources.note: Court evidence for Ranjit Singh's patronage and costs.

sources.citation: Pardeep Singh Arshi, The Golden Temple: History, Art and Architecture (1989)
sources.note: Standard architectural study of Harmandir Sahib's phases and design.

sources.citation: W.G. Osborne, The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing (1840); J.M. Honigberger, Thirty-Five Years in the East (1852)
sources.note: European eyewitness descriptions of the shrine and court.

episodes.notes: The Harmandir Sahib had been damaged and rebuilt through the 18th century before Ranjit Singh controlled Amritsar in 1802. He funded marble work and, by about 1830, the gold overlay that gave the shrine its popular name, while the four entrances and low sanctum expressed openness and humility. This is a craft, economic and devotional story: treasury, artisanship, Mughal-Sikh design synthesis and public sacred space. RECENT/ACCURACY FLAGS: conservation studies stress many rebuilding phases; gold quantities vary, so avoid exact weights; pre-1984 Akal Takht murals documented by Kanwarjit Singh Kang were later destroyed, so do NOT imply all older artwork survives unchanged.
episodes.chapter: The Sikh Gurus and Ranjit Singh

episodes.title: The Doctor Who Built a Science House
episodes.era: Colonial Bengal and the founding of IACS, 1867-1876
episodes.region: Calcutta, Bengal Presidency
episodes.logline: Mahendralal Sarkar turns public donations into India's first independent research institute, proving that Indians can build science on their own terms.
episodes.moral: Institutions begin when one person refuses to wait for permission.

sources.citation: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science founding deed and minute books, 1876, IACS Archives, Kolkata
sources.note: Primary institutional record for the association founded on 29 July 1876.

sources.citation: Mahendralal Sarkar, Calcutta Journal of Medicine, from 1868
sources.note: Shows Sarkar's medical and scientific advocacy in print.

sources.citation: Deepak Kumar, Science and the Raj 1857-1905, Oxford University Press, 1995
sources.note: Places IACS within colonial exclusion from official scientific bodies and Indian public science efforts.

episodes.notes: Mahendralal Sarkar, the second MD graduate of Calcutta Medical College, campaigned from 1867 until the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science opened on 29 July 1876 in Calcutta. This is a SOCIAL and INSTITUTIONAL innovation story: a science institution funded by Indian public subscription rather than colonial patronage. It later gave C.V. Raman the laboratory space where the Raman Effect was found. Recent work by Deepak Kumar and Projit Mukharji reads Sarkar's project as both scientific self-strengthening and part of colonial Bengal's medical politics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim IACS was the first non-European science institution in the world; the safer attested claim is first Indian-run independent research institution. Sarkar also defended homeopathy, so present him as a complex medical reformer, not a modern laboratory scientist in every respect.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Dawn of Indian Research

episodes.title: The Chemist Who Made Swadeshi Medicine
episodes.region: Calcutta, Edinburgh and Maniktala
episodes.logline: Prafulla Chandra Ray turns a home laboratory into Bengal Chemical, joining modern chemistry with the dream of Indian industrial self-reliance.
episodes.moral: Knowledge serves best when it also builds livelihoods.

sources.citation: Prafulla Chandra Ray, Life and Experiences of a Bengali Chemist, 2 vols., 1932 and 1935
sources.note: Primary memoir for Ray's training, teaching and Bengal Chemical.

sources.citation: Prafulla Chandra Ray, History of Hindu Chemistry, vols. 1-2, 1902 and 1908
sources.note: Ray's own scholarly recovery of earlier Indian chemical traditions.

sources.citation: John Lourdusamy, Science and National Consciousness in Bengal 1870-1930, Orient Longman, 2004
sources.note: Recent study of Ray's pedagogy, nationalism and student network.

episodes.notes: Ray returned from Edinburgh to Presidency College, published his 1896 study of mercurous nitrite, and in 1901 founded Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works from modest rooms in Calcutta. This is an ECONOMIC and SCHOLARLY innovation story: an Indian pharmaceutical enterprise making medicines and chemicals, and a historian-chemist using Sanskrit sources in History of Hindu Chemistry. His students included Meghnad Saha and S.N. Bose. Recent scholarship by Lourdusamy and Projit Mukharji stresses the mix of modern lab science, swadeshi industry and historical recovery. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Ray invented mercurous nitrite from nothing; say he systematically synthesized and studied it in an Indian laboratory. Do NOT portray him as an armed freedom fighter; his nationalism was industrial, educational and scholarly.
episodes.chapter_part: I. The Dawn of Indian Research

episodes.title: Bose Sends Invisible Waves Through Walls
episodes.region: Presidency College and Bose Institute, Calcutta
episodes.logline: Jagadish Chandra Bose builds tiny instruments, sends millimetre waves through walls, and then measures the hidden pulses of plants.
episodes.moral: Curiosity can cross the border between machines and life.

sources.citation: J.C. Bose, On Polarisation of Electric Rays by Double-Refracting Crystals, The Electrician, 1895
sources.note: Primary publication from Bose's millimetre-wave experiments.

sources.citation: J.C. Bose, Response in the Living and Non-Living, Longmans Green, 1902
sources.note: Primary source for his plant and biophysical investigations.

sources.citation: Subrata Dasgupta, Jagadish Chandra Bose and the Indian Response to Western Science, Oxford University Press, 1999
sources.note: Modern contextual biography of Bose's physics, biology and colonial setting.

episodes.notes: Bose demonstrated millimetre-range waves in Calcutta in the 1890s using apparatus he built while facing salary discrimination at Presidency College. He later studied plant responses with instruments such as the crescograph and founded the Bose Institute in 1917. This is a SCIENTIFIC and ENGINEERING innovation story: horn antennas, waveguides and a galena detector anticipated parts of microwave and semiconductor practice, while his plant work helped create a biophysical imagination. IEEE recognition in 1998 and later history-of-science work have restored his technical importance. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim Bose invented radio before Marconi; Bose studied the physics of waves, not commercial wireless telegraphy. Do NOT claim Marconi simply stole Bose's invention; priority and influence remain debated.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Minds That Changed the World

episodes.title: Ramanujan Posts a Letter of Theorems
episodes.region: Erode, Kumbakonam, Madras and Cambridge
episodes.logline: A clerk in Madras mails G.H. Hardy pages of strange theorems, and the world of number theory opens a door no one knew was there.
episodes.moral: Genius still needs someone willing to read carefully.

sources.citation: Srinivasa Ramanujan's letter to G.H. Hardy, 16 January 1913, Trinity College Library, Cambridge, MS R.1.1
sources.note: Primary surviving letter that launched the Cambridge collaboration.

sources.citation: G.H. Hardy and S. Ramanujan, Asymptotic formulae in combinatory analysis, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society 17, 1918
sources.note: Primary partition-function paper.

sources.citation: George Andrews and Bruce Berndt, Ramanujan's Lost Notebook, 5 vols., Springer, 2005-2013
sources.note: Definitive recent edition and analysis of the final notebook material.

episodes.notes: Ramanujan's 16 January 1913 letter to Hardy contained more than a hundred results, some known and many astonishingly new. At Cambridge he worked on partitions, modular forms, continued fractions and related fields; he became FRS in 1918 and in his last 1920 letter introduced mock theta functions. This is a MATHEMATICAL and SCHOLARLY innovation story whose recent afterlife includes Andrews and Berndt's lost-notebook editions and work by Ken Ono and others linking mock theta functions to modern mathematics and physics. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT present family traditions about the goddess Namagiri giving theorems in dreams as verified fact. Do NOT say vegetarianism in England caused his death; later medical reassessment points strongly to hepatic amoebiasis contracted earlier.
episodes.chapter_part: II. Minds That Changed the World

episodes.title: Light Scatters in Raman's Calcutta Lab
episodes.region: Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Calcutta
episodes.logline: In a modest Calcutta laboratory, C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan catch light changing colour as it passes through matter.
episodes.moral: Great discovery can begin with simple tools and disciplined eyes.

sources.citation: C.V. Raman and K.S. Krishnan, A New Type of Secondary Radiation, Nature 121, 31 March 1928
sources.note: Primary discovery announcement of the Raman Effect.

sources.citation: C.V. Raman, The Molecular Scattering of Light, Nobel Lecture, 11 December 1930
sources.note: Raman's official Nobel account of the discovery and its meaning.

sources.citation: Abha Sur, Dispersed Radiance: Caste, Gender and Modern Science in India, Navayana, 2011
sources.note: Recent critique emphasizing laboratory hierarchies and K.S. Krishnan's role.

episodes.notes: Raman's voyage across the Mediterranean inspired questions about light scattering, but the discovery itself happened in the IACS laboratory in Calcutta in February 1928. The Nature paper of 31 March 1928 named both Raman and K.S. Krishnan; Raman received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation story: Raman spectroscopy now serves chemistry, medicine, materials science and forensics. Recent scholarship by Abha Sur and Rajinder Singh stresses Krishnan's under-credited work and the Russian parallel of Landsberg and Mandelstam. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT make the blue-sea moment the discovery. Do NOT present the Raman Effect as Raman's sole, unaided finding; Krishnan was a key co-worker even though the Nobel went only to Raman.

episodes.title: Bose Writes the Statistics of Light
episodes.region: Dhaka, Berlin and Calcutta
episodes.logline: Satyendra Nath Bose sends Einstein a rejected paper that teaches physics how to count light quanta as indistinguishable particles.
episodes.moral: A rejected idea may still change the rules of the universe.

sources.citation: S.N. Bose, Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese, Zeitschrift fuer Physik 26, 1924
sources.note: Primary paper translated and submitted by Einstein.

sources.citation: S.N. Bose's letter to Albert Einstein, 1924, Einstein Archives, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, catalogue 6-340
sources.note: Primary correspondence behind the publication.

sources.citation: Jagdish Mehra and Helmut Rechenberg, The Historical Development of Quantum Theory, vol. 5, Springer, 2000
sources.note: Modern quantum-history context for Bose's derivation and Einstein's extension.

episodes.notes: At Dhaka University in 1924, Bose derived Planck's law by counting photons as indistinguishable particles. After rejection by Philosophical Magazine, he sent the paper to Einstein, who translated it into German, endorsed it, and extended the idea to atoms; Dirac later named bosons for Bose. This is a SCIENTIFIC and MATHEMATICAL innovation story whose importance was renewed after the 1995 creation of Bose-Einstein condensates and the 2001 Nobel for that experimental work. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Einstein stole Bose's idea; Einstein cited and extended it. Do NOT state Bose deserved a Nobel more than someone else; the omission is a historical debate, not a proof of theft.

episodes.title: Chandra Finds the Weight of Dead Stars
episodes.region: Madras, Cambridge and Chicago
episodes.logline: On a ship to England, young Chandrasekhar calculates that a white dwarf above a limit must collapse toward stranger fates.
episodes.moral: Truth may need patience when authority says no.

sources.citation: S. Chandrasekhar, The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs, Astrophysical Journal 74, 1931
sources.note: Primary early publication of the stellar mass limit.

sources.citation: S. Chandrasekhar, On Stars, Their Evolution and Their Stability, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1983
sources.note: Official retrospective by Chandrasekhar on the theory's meaning.

sources.citation: Kameshwar C. Wali, Chandra: A Biography of S. Chandrasekhar, University of Chicago Press, 1991
sources.note: Definitive biography drawing on interviews and correspondence.

episodes.notes: Chandrasekhar calculated the white-dwarf mass limit during his 1930 voyage from India to Cambridge and published the result in 1931; his 1935 Royal Astronomical Society presentation met famous resistance from Arthur Eddington. The result later became foundational for neutron stars, black holes and Type Ia supernovae, and Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation and a credit-resistance story. Recent biographies and Arthur Miller's Empire of the Stars debate whether Eddington's opposition included racial assumptions. ACCURACY FLAGS: present racial motivation as debated, not settled fact. Do NOT claim he would certainly have won the Nobel in 1935; scientific acceptance and Nobel politics were more complex.

episodes.title: Saha Reads the Temperature of Stars
episodes.era: Saha ionization equation and science advocacy, 1920-1956
episodes.region: Calcutta, Allahabad and Parliament in New Delhi
episodes.logline: Meghnad Saha turns heat, pressure and atoms into an equation that lets astronomers read the hidden temperatures of stars.
episodes.moral: A clear equation can turn scattered clues into understanding.

sources.citation: M.N. Saha, Ionisation in the Solar Chromosphere, Philosophical Magazine 40, 1920
sources.note: Primary first paper on the ionization equation.

sources.citation: M.N. Saha, On a Physical Theory of Stellar Spectra, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 99, 1921
sources.note: Primary fuller derivation and astrophysical application.

sources.citation: Virendra Nath Sharma, Meghnad Saha: His Life and Times, Rupa, 2019
sources.note: Recent full biography situating Saha's science and public policy work.

episodes.notes: Born near Dhaka, Saha used thermodynamics and atomic physics in 1920-21 to explain why stellar spectra vary with temperature and pressure. His ionization equation made modern stellar classification quantitative and later supported plasma physics. He also founded Science and Culture, helped establish the Institute of Nuclear Physics, and entered Parliament to argue for scientific planning. This is a SCIENTIFIC innovation story with institutional and civic dimensions. Recent scholarship stresses both Western textbook under-recognition and Saha's public role in river and energy planning. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say Saha worked without Western physics; his originality lay in combining existing thermodynamics and atomic theory. Do NOT frame Nobel non-recognition as a proven robbery; it is a documented recognition gap.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers
