episodes.title: Mahalanobis Measures a Nation
episodes.region: Calcutta and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis builds the Indian Statistical Institute and teaches a new nation how to count crops, distances and plans.
episodes.moral: Good decisions need good measurements.

sources.citation: P.C. Mahalanobis, On the Generalised Distance in Statistics, Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2, 1936
sources.note: Primary paper introducing Mahalanobis distance.

sources.citation: P.C. Mahalanobis, On Large-Scale Sample Surveys, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 231, 1944
sources.note: Primary major paper on sample survey design.

sources.citation: Arup Banerji, Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis, National Book Trust, 1997
sources.note: Standard biography of Mahalanobis and the ISI.

episodes.notes: Mahalanobis founded the Indian Statistical Institute in a room at Presidency College on 17 December 1931, developed the Mahalanobis distance, and pioneered large-scale sample surveys for crop and social data. After independence he joined the Planning Commission and shaped the statistical framework behind the Second Five Year Plan. This is an ECONOMIC, STATISTICAL and INSTITUTIONAL innovation story: measurement became statecraft. Recent economic histories, including critiques in Economic and Political Weekly, reassess the heavy-industry bias of the Mahalanobis model without denying his survey genius. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say he invented statistics; he made major contributions to multivariate distance, survey sampling and Indian statistical institutions. Do NOT present planning outcomes as unanimously successful.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers

episodes.title: Janaki Ammal Counts Sugarcane Chromosomes
episodes.region: Thalassery, Michigan, Coimbatore, Britain and Allahabad
episodes.logline: Janaki Ammal studies chromosomes in sugarcane and garden plants, helping Indian agriculture while opening doors for women in science.
episodes.moral: Patient work in living cells can nourish a country.

sources.citation: Janaki Ammal, Chromosome Studies in Nicandra Physaloides, PhD thesis, University of Michigan, 1931
sources.note: Primary doctoral work documenting her cytogenetic training.

sources.citation: C.D. Darlington and Janaki Ammal, Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants, George Allen and Unwin, 1945
sources.note: Landmark co-authored cytogenetics reference.

sources.citation: Gita Chadha, Janaki Ammal: Science in the Service of Life, in Feminism in India, Zubaan, 2008
sources.note: Recent feminist science-studies account of her career and erasure.

episodes.notes: Janaki Ammal earned a Michigan PhD in 1931, worked at the Sugarcane Breeding Station in Coimbatore from the 1930s, and used cytogenetics and polyploidy to support hardier sugarcane breeding for Indian conditions. During World War II she worked at the John Innes Institute and co-authored Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants in 1945; after independence she led the Central Botanical Laboratory and later supported Silent Valley conservation. This is a SCIENTIFIC, AGRICULTURAL and SOCIAL innovation story. Recent feminist scholarship highlights how women scientists' records were scattered or unnamed. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say she saved India's sugar industry single-handedly; she contributed to a larger breeding program. Specific Coimbatore variety attributions are sometimes poorly preserved.
episodes.chapter_part: IV. Science for Land, Life and Numbers

episodes.title: Bhabha Draws a Map of Atomic India
episodes.region: Bombay, Bangalore, Trombay and New Delhi
episodes.logline: Homi Bhabha writes to Tata and Nehru, then builds TIFR and an atomic-energy programme for a newly independent nation.
episodes.moral: A bold institution can turn talent into national capacity.

sources.citation: H.J. Bhabha's letter to the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, 1944, TIFR Archives, Mumbai
sources.note: Primary proposal for a national institute of fundamental research.

sources.citation: H.J. Bhabha and W. Heitler, The Passage of Fast Electrons and the Theory of Cosmic Showers, Proceedings of the Royal Society A 159, 1937
sources.note: Primary scientific work on cosmic ray showers.

sources.citation: Indira Chowdhury and Ananya Dasgupta, A Masterful Spirit: Homi J. Bhabha, 1909-1966, Penguin India, 2010
sources.note: Archival biography of Bhabha and TIFR.

episodes.notes: Bhabha trained at Cambridge, produced important work on electron-positron scattering and cosmic ray showers, and in 1944 proposed a Tata-backed institute for fundamental research. TIFR opened in Bombay in 1945; the Atomic Energy Commission followed in 1948, and Trombay became the centre of India's nuclear establishment. This is an ENGINEERING, INSTITUTIONAL and economic-development innovation story, especially through the three-stage nuclear-power vision based on India's thorium resources. Recent scholarship using TIFR archives debates whether the thorium programme was visionary or over-optimistic. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT call Bhabha the father of India's nuclear bomb; his public programme emphasized peaceful atomic energy, and the 1974 test came after his death. Do NOT repeat Mont Blanc crash sabotage rumours as fact.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation

episodes.title: Sarabhai Launches from a Fisherman's Shore
episodes.region: Ahmedabad, Thumba and Thiruvananthapuram
episodes.logline: Vikram Sarabhai turns a church near the magnetic equator into the launch site for India's first sounding rocket.
episodes.moral: Science reaches higher when it serves everyday life below.

sources.citation: INCOSPAR founding documents, 1962, Department of Space and ISRO records
sources.note: Primary institutional record for the committee that began India's space programme.

sources.citation: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam and Arun Tiwari, Wings of Fire, Universities Press, 1999
sources.note: Firsthand account of the Thumba years and early rocket work.

sources.citation: Amrita Shah, Vikram Sarabhai: A Life, Penguin Viking, 2007
sources.note: Standard biography using PRL archives and family records.

episodes.notes: Sarabhai founded the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad on 11 November 1947, led INCOSPAR from 1962, and chose Thumba because it lay near the magnetic equator. With local church support, St. Mary Magdalene Church became a rocket assembly space, and India launched a US Nike-Apache sounding rocket on 21 November 1963; the Indian-designed Rohini RH-75 followed in 1967. This is an ENGINEERING and DEVELOPMENT innovation story: Sarabhai argued space research should support communication, weather, education and agriculture. Recent ISRO and VSSC retrospectives preserve photographs and launch records, including the bicycle nose-cone tradition. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT say the first rocket was Indian-designed. Do NOT say Sarabhai founded ISRO directly; INCOSPAR became ISRO in 1972 after his death.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation

episodes.title: Bhatnagar Builds the National Labs
episodes.region: Lahore, Delhi, Pune, Mysore, Dhanbad and Lucknow
episodes.logline: Shanti Swaroop Bhatnagar helps turn CSIR into a network of laboratories for food, fuel, drugs, physics and industry.
episodes.moral: A nation grows stronger when research is shared across many workshops.

sources.citation: CSIR founding records and annual reports, 1942-1954, CSIR Archives and Government of India records
sources.note: Primary institutional evidence for Bhatnagar's laboratory programme.

sources.citation: S.S. Bhatnagar and K.N. Mathur, Physical Principles and Applications of Magnetochemistry, Macmillan, 1935
sources.note: Primary scientific monograph representing Bhatnagar's research field.

sources.citation: INSA, Biographical Memoir of S.S. Bhatnagar, Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of INSA, vol. 4, 1960
sources.note: Institutional scholarly memoir with career chronology.

episodes.notes: Bhatnagar was a chemist, magnetochemistry researcher, poet and administrator. After becoming CSIR's first Director-General in 1942, he worked with Nehru to build national laboratories after independence, including the National Physical Laboratory, National Chemical Laboratory, Central Food Technological Research Institute, Central Fuel Research Institute and Central Drug Research Institute. This is an INSTITUTIONAL, ECONOMIC and INDUSTRIAL innovation story: science policy became a network of practical research centres. Recent postcolonial histories debate whether CSIR created independent research capacity or leaned too much on adaptation of foreign technology. ACCURACY FLAGS: do NOT claim every laboratory was world-class immediately; many began short of staff and equipment. His legacy is the framework, momentum and national laboratory vision.
episodes.chapter_part: V. Laboratories of a Free Nation
